en: Salutations to Śrī Sarasvatī. Now begins the *Pariṣkāradarpaṇa*.
May there be auspiciousness.
Having bowed to Śiva together with Ambā and having meditated upon the lotus feet of the gurus,
we compose this Mirror of Refinements for the sake of effortless awakening.
Even for those possessed of scriptural knowledge and wisdom, there is a lack of splendor without the necessary requisites;
having reflected upon the ultimate limit of suffering, this treatise is composed. (2)
Furthermore, a stream of refinements following the true tradition expands the science of grammar;
for a beautiful heroine, devoid of ornaments, never shines at all in the world. (3)
Thus the science of grammar shines forth, uninterrupted by any stream of refinements;
having reflected thus, I compose this work which is always difficult for grammarians to endure. (4)
Having exerted effort amidst the clusters of forest-thickets of the scriptures, situated between Kāśī and Prayāga as his lower and middle limits,
he joyfully composes this work, abundant with a multitude of refinements, for the delight of the virtuous and for their sustenance.
I, Śukla Sarayūpārīṇa, known by the name Veṇīmādhava,
repeatedly offer this floral tribute to the virtuous.
Having praised my mother and father, as well as my supreme teacher Jayadeva, I compose this work; may Hari bestow auspiciousness.

Now, regarding the question of what is an object (*viṣaya*) and what is objectivity (*viṣayatā*), here is the answer: it is called an *object* (*viṣaya*) because it "binds" (*viṣiṇoti*)—that is, it binds the subject (*viṣayin*) by making itself determinable through its own form. The verbal root is *ṣiñ* (to bind) preceded by the prefix *vi-*. The suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *nandigrahipacādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.134]. It is stated that "the object ranges from the binary atomic compound (*dvyaṇuka*) up to the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). The general definition of being an object is "the state of being a means for experience."

The fundamental position is that all categories of objects (padārtha) possess the state of being denoted (vācyatā), as defined by the denotative capacity (vācakatā) residing in words signifying objects. Now, it will be explained later that even God is not denotable by the word "object" (viṣaya), because He is distinct from the world, because He is unmanifest (avyakta), and because He is the object of specific knowledge (viśiṣṭajñāna). Objectivity (viṣayatā) is a specific attribute (dharmaviśeṣa) defined by knowledge and so forth, which is distinct from the object of knowledge itself. Essential nature (svarūpa) is twofold: the essential nature of ignorance (ajñāna-svarūpa) and the essential nature of the object (viṣaya-svarūpa).

There is the cognition having the jar as its object, and the jar is the object of that cognition; first there is the awareness where the cognition has the jar as its counter-correlate (pratiyogin) and the jar is its sub-correlate (anuyogin), and subsequently there is the awareness where the jar has the cognition as its counter-correlate and the cognition is its sub-correlate, due to the lack of any decisive factor [to prefer one over the other]. That both the jar and the cognition possess the status of being a counter-correlate and a sub-correlate [respectively] is common knowledge among all people.

Objection: Let it be that the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*) is simply the very nature of the object, such as a jar. Reply: No; for if objecthood were the very nature of the object like a jar, then the relationship between the container and the contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) between the object and its objecthood would be untenable. Furthermore, since identity (*abheda*) does not serve as a determinant of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*), the conventional usage "the jar possesses the objecthood of cognition" (*ghaṭo jñānaviṣayatāvān*) would be impossible. Nor can it be argued that even identity constitutes the relationship of container and contained; for if that were so, the unavoidable consequence would be the cognition "the jar possesses [itself]" (*ghaṭavān*), just as one might say "the jar possesses the objecthood of cognition. Therefore, objecthood is indeed of the same nature as the cognition itself.

Some, however, maintain that objectivity (*viṣayatā*) consists of both the cognition and its object; yet in reality, objectivity is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) altogether, and not of the nature of both cognition and object. In such cases as "the jar possesses the genus [jar-ness]," it would be untenable for the single objectivity residing in a single object (the jar) to possess a twofold character—namely, being non-delimited by the property of "genus-ness" and being delimited by the property of "genus-ness"—simultaneously, because the cognition and the object are one and the same. Therefore, according to this established doctrine, objectivity is indeed distinct from both the cognition and the object.

Just as the objectness (*viṣayatā*) is distinct, so too is the relation between the object and its correlate called "object-ness" (*anuyogitā*) distinct; and the relation between the cognition and its correlate called "counter-correlateness" (*pratiyogitā*) is distinct. This is because, even if the nature of the cognition and the object were identical, there would be no distinction [between them] due to the difference between the two relations.

Just as knowledge possesses an object and cannot be objectless—since knowledge is eternally dependent upon an object—so too, if the object were likewise to possess an object, it would follow that just as the pot is the object of knowledge, so knowledge would be the object of the pot. Therefore, there must be something distinct from both knowledge and its object, namely what is called the *anuyogitā* (the correlate) and the *pratiyogitā* (the counter-correlate).
Now, what is the meaning of the terms *anuyogitā* and *pratiyogitā*?
Regarding the word *pratiyogī*: previously there was a "yoga" or relation; that which has such a relation is a *pratiyogī*. The state of being a *pratiyogī* is *pratiyogitā*.
Anu means "subsequent" (paścāt); that which has a connection (yoga), meaning a relationship (sambandha), with this [subsequent element] is called *anuyogin*.

Anuyogitā (the state of being the correlate) is the property of being the substratum (*anuyogin*). For example, in the case of "the pot is blue" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) resides in the blue, while the anuyogitā resides in the pot. In the case of "the pot is the object of knowledge" (*jñānaviṣayo ghaṭaḥ*), the counter-correlativity resides in the knowledge, while the anuyogitā resides in the pot. In the case of "the pot does not exist" (*ghaṭo nāsti*), the counter-correlativity resides in the pot, while the anuyogitā resides in the absence (*abhāva*). Similarly, the relation of objecthood (*viṣayitā*) is also distinct, consisting of a relation between the object and the knowledge as its substratum. The relation of the knowledge to the object is called objectivity (*viṣayatā*).

The essential meaning is that the relation between an object and its cognition is termed "objectivity" (*viṣayatā*). Objectivity differs according to the difference in objects; it does not vary with the difference in cognitions. Even though cognitions are distinct due to differences in persons and so forth, only a single jar appears within the cognition.

And consider the following examples: "Maitra is the son of Caitra" and "Caitra is the son of Maitra. What is the difference between these two cognitions? In the first sentence, the objects are Caitra-ness and Caitra; in the second sentence as well, there is complete equality in the enumeration of objects. It is precisely from a difference in objects that a difference in cognition arises. For instance, in the case of "Devadatta’s son" and "Yajñadatta’s father," there is an even greater difference between these two cognitions.

The distinction is that in the former sentence the subject matter consists of Devadatta-ness, being the son of Devadatta, and so forth, whereas in the latter sentence the subject matter consists of Yajñadatta-ness, being the father of Yajñadatta, and so forth. The method for investigating the difference between these two sentences is as follows.

In the cognition "Caitra’s son is Maitra," there is the relation with the referent of the word *maitra*, which is either the qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) or the subjecthood (*dharmitā*); with respect to being-Maitra (*maitratva*), it is the delimiting property of qualificandness (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatā*) or the delimiting property of subjecthood (*dharmitāvacchedakatā*); with respect to Caitra, it is the qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatā*) or the modehood (*prakāratā*); with respect to being-Caitra (*caitratva*), it is the delimiting property of qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedakatā*) or the delimiting property of modehood (*prakāratāvacchedakatā*); and with respect to inherence (*samavāya*), it is the delimiting property of the modehood of the relational [content] (*sāṃsargikaprakāratāvacchedakatā*).

Alternatively, in the cognition "Caitra is the son of Maitra," there is the state of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) in Caitra, and the state of being the delimitor of the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatā*) in the property of being Caitra (*caitratva*). In the former cognition, there is the state of being the delimitor of the qualifier (*prakāratāvacchedakatā*) in *caitratva*; in the second cognition, there is the state of being the qualifier (*prakāratā*) in Maitra, the state of being the delimitor of the qualifier (*prakāratāvacchedakatā*) in the property of being Maitra (*maitratva*), and the state of being the delimitor of the delimitor of the qualifier (*prakāratāvacchedakatāvacchedakatā*) in inherence (*samavāya*), or rather, the state of being the delimitor of the relational qualifier (*sāṃsargikaprakāratāvacchedakatā*) in inherence.
Thus, because there exist infinite relations such as fitness (*yogyatā*), there is a distinction between the meanings of the sentences.

There is one temporal relation (*kālikasambandha*); by means of it, all categories (*padārtha*) exist everywhere. Here, even in the absence of temporality (*kālikatā*), general relations such as "existence" (*asti*) and so forth should be inferred in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and other entities, either through the temporal relation itself or through the relation of being located in its own time (*svakālādheyatva*).

In a sentence where there is a mutual relationship of particulars (*viśeṣa*) and not a relationship of universals (*sāmānya*), there is determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), or it is called "determinate. Where there is only a relationship of universals such as time and so forth, and no particularity, there is indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), or it is called "indeterminate."

It is a rule that non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) is the cause of conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*). Non-conceptual knowledge is simply the distinct cognition of each [element], devoid of the relation [between them], such as "pot" and "pot-ness. Subsequently, when there is knowledge of inherence (*samavāya*), conceptual knowledge arises; conceptual knowledge is precisely the knowledge of the relationship between multiple categories—this is the rule. Knowledge is threefold: conceptual, non-conceptual, and that which consists of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*).

The nature of being a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) consists in being a cognition that does not possess a subject-object relationship (*viṣayatā*) wherein the objects stand in the relation of the perceived and the perceiver toward one another—as in the case of "the jar [is related] to the cloth."

Specific relations (*viśeṣasaṃbandha*) include, for example: the state of being a substratum (*ādhāratva*), the state of being contained (*ādheyatva*), the state of being a locus (*āśrayatva*), the state of being located (*āśrayitva*), the state of being dependent (*āśritatva*), the state of being produced (*janyatva*), the state of being a producer (*janakatva*), the state of ownership (*svatva*), the state of being an owner (*svāmitva*), the state of being a definitor (*nirūpakatva*), the state of being defined (*nirūpitatva*), the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*), the state of being a subject (*viṣayitva*), the state of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*), the state of being a part (*avayavatva*), the state of being a whole (*avayavitva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), essential nature (*svarūpa*), and so forth. In the expression "the space within a jar" (*ghaṭākāśaḥ*) and "the midday heat" (*jyeṣṭhātapaḥ*), there is a relation of being delimited (*avacchedyatvasaṃbandha*) between the jar and the space, and a relation of being delimited between the midday sun and the heat.

"A man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*) is a qualificandumhood delimited by "man-ness" (*puruṣatva*), which is determined by a qualifierhood delimited by "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) and conditioned by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

"The ground possesses a jar" (*ghaṭavad bhūtalam*) is a qualificandumhood delimited by "ground-ness," which is determined by a qualifierhood delimited by "jar-ness" and conditioned by the relation of conjunction. In the case of "there is no fruit on the tree," the relation of the absence of fruit to the tree is one of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

Although the tree possesses the status of a locus (*ādhāratva*) with respect to the absence of fruit, and the absence of fruit possesses the status of being located (*ādheyatva*) in the tree, nevertheless, in every such case, there exists some distinct relation that acts as their regulator, determiner, delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), restrictor, indicator, or establisher. For example, in the cognition "the ground is possessed of a jar" (*ghaṭavad bhūtalam*), although the pure understanding is simply that the ground possesses a locus-ness defined by the located-ness residing in the jar, nevertheless, the contact (*saṃyoga*) serves as its delimiting factor. In the case of "the absence of a jar on the ground," the relation that regulates the state of locus and located is the relation of identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

Objection: Just as there is the statement "the ground possesses a jar," why do such formulations as "the jar possesses the ground," "the jar possesses color," "the mountain possesses a jar," "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," or "the absence of a jar possesses the ground" not also occur? For relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) are defined by both relata. Reply: This is not so; for even in the case of relations consisting of conjunction, inherence (*samavāya*), or identity (*svarūpa*), there exists some further relation that serves as their determiner.

Among these relations, there are two types of objects: the relation known as *anuyogitā* (substratumness) and that known as *pratiyogitā* (counter-correlativeness). If, in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other such relations, there is *anuyogitā*, then there is a cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭabodha*). Where there is only the relation of *pratiyogitā*, there is no cognition of the qualified.

In the expression "the ground possesses a jar" (*ghaṭavad bhūtalam*), there is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between the jar and the ground; the factor that determines this [conjunction] is the state of being the locus (*anuyogitva*) residing in the ground. Therefore, it occurs that "the ground possesses a jar," but it does not occur that "the jar possesses the ground. This is because the relation in the jar is the state of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*), due to the absence of the state of being the locus.

One says "the jar possesses milk," but one does not say "the milk possesses the jar. Although conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is indeed equal in both cases, nevertheless, by the force of cognition, the jar alone is the locus (*anuyogin*), while the milk alone is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); therefore, it is only said that "the jar possesses milk. In the same way, there is an inherence (*samavāya*) between qualities such as color and taste, and substances such as gold and mangoes, respectively.

However, the property of being the substratum (anuyogitva) that determines the inherence relation between a quality and a substance exists only in the substance, not in the quality and so forth; for this very reason, one says "gold possesses color" or "the mango fruit possesses taste," but one does not say "color possesses gold" or "taste possesses the mango fruit. Furthermore, there is a mutual inherence relation between action and the substances Caitra and Maitra; here, the property of being the substratum that determines the inherence relation exists [in the agent], and thus one says "Maitra possesses motion" or "Caitra possesses speech."

Is it not the case that movement is like that of Maitra and speech is like that of Caitra? No, because there is an absence of an action that determines the state of being the subject of the inquiry (*anuyogitva*).

Although the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) exists mutually between a pot and a cloth and so forth, nevertheless, the status of being the locus (*anuyogitva*) that regulates the inherence resides in the parts (*avayava*), while the status of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) resides in the whole (*avayavin*). Therefore, linguistic usages such as "the threads possess the cloth" or "the potsherds possess the pot" occur; however, expressions such as "the cloth possesses the threads" or "the pot possesses the potsherds" do not occur, due to the reasoning stated previously. In cases such as "the king's man," the regulator or determiner of ownership (*svatva*) is also present: the locus-ness resides in the man, while the counter-correlate-ness resides in the king.

In the expression "a golden pot" (*suvarṇaghaṭaḥ*), there is the state of being produced (*janyatva*) in the pot with respect to gold; this is the relation (*saṃsarga*). Its relatum-ship (*anuyogitva*) resides in the pot, while its counter-correlate-ship (*pratiyogitva*) resides in the gold. The essential meaning is that counter-correlate-ship takes the form of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), and relatum-ship takes the form of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*).

The qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) is of two kinds: delimited (*sāvacchinnā*) and undelimited (*niravacchinnā*). In the cognition "This is a jar" (*ayaṃ ghaṭaḥ*), the qualificand-ness residing in the jar, which is determined by the mode-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in jar-ness, is delimited by "this-ness" (*idantva*). In the cognition whose form is simply "jar" (*kevalaghaṭaḥ*), the qualificand-ness residing in the jar, which is determined by the mode-ness residing in jar-ness, is undelimited. In the former cognition, "this-ness" and so forth alone constitute the delimitor of the subjecthood (*dharmmitāvacchedaka*); for the term "delimitor of subjecthood" (*dharmmitāvacchedakatā*) signifies precisely the status of being a delimitor of the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatā*).

The modehood (*prakāratā*) is also of two kinds: delimited (*sāvacchinnā*) and undelimited (*niravacchinnā*). In a cognition having the form "this is a jar" (*ghaṭa iti*), since the property of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth exists in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), the modehood residing in jar-ness—determined by the qualificandumhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the jar—is undelimited. In cases such as "the house possesses a jar," the modehood residing in the jar—determined by the qualificandumhood residing in the house and delimited by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—is delimited by jar-ness.

The property of being the subject (*uddeśyatā*) and the property of being the predicate (*vidheyatā*) are also, like the property of being an object (*viṣayatā*), distinct [from their relata]. For example, in the case of "The mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*), there is a qualificandness delimited by mountain-ness, which is determined by a qualifier-ness delimited by fire-ness and delimited by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Here, the property of being the predicate resides in the fire, and the property of being the subject resides in the mountain.
And as for "being delimited" (*avacchinnatvam*):

Just as in the case of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) and reality (*tattva*), in the case of objecthood (*viṣayatā*) and so forth as well, there is only a specific relation for *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) and the like. What is the meaning of the expression "objecthood delimited by pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvāvacchinnā viṣayatā*)? It means an objecthood that possesses a delimitedness (*avacchedyatā*) which is itself qualified by a delimitingness (*avacchedakatā*) residing in pot-ness.

And delimitingness (*avacchedakatva*) is the state of being a delimiter when it is both denotable (*śakyatva*) and capable of differentiating the denoted from others (*śakyavyāvarttakatva*). For example, in "the pot" (*ghaṭa*) and similar cases, pot-ness is denotable by the word "pot" and it differentiates the referent from the referents of words such as "cloth."

The state of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) consists in being neither less nor more pervasive, or alternatively, in being that which does not reside in anything less nor in anything more. For instance, in the case of "this is a jar," the property of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) does not reside in anything less than a jar, nor does it reside in anything more; rather, it resides in every jar. Thus, jar-ness is the delimiting factor. Herein is the essential point: delimiting factor-ness is a specific type of essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*), and in some cases, it consists in being a property that serves as the qualifier within the portion of the counter-positive (*pratiyogyaṃśa*).

Just as, for example, the property of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) belongs to "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) with respect to the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absence of the object of cognition (smoke); in some cases, however, it is the property of not occurring in anything other than that (*anatiriktavṛttitva*). And this is of two kinds. Among these, the first is: being a non-counter-correlative of an absence that occurs in the locus of that [property], while at the same time not occurring in anything devoid of that [property]. For example, the property of being a delimiting factor belongs to "potness" (*ghaṭatva*) with respect to the counter-correlativity of the absence of a pot.

The second [type of delimitation], however, is the state of being qualified by some property through a triple relation consisting of: (1) being a delimiter (*vyāvarttakatva*), (2) co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and (3) having its own locus as that which is delimited (*svaniṣṭhāvacchedyatākattva*). For example, the stick possesses the status of being the delimiter for the causal efficiency of a jar. In some cases, however, it is the locus of that [property] which possesses the status of being the delimiter for the property residing therein; for instance, in such expressions as "there is no contact with a monkey on the tree at the root, but [it is] on the branch," the branch and so forth—which are loci of the tree—possess the status of being the delimiters for the contact with a monkey residing in the tree.

Or, for example, in the case of "The fire is on the slope of this mountain, not on the peak," the property of being the slope (*nitamba*) functions as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the presence of the fire, whereas the property of being the peak functions as the delimiting factor for the absence of the fire. Likewise, in cases such as "There is no cow in the courtyard now," even the property of being the present time (*etatkāla*) serves as the delimiting factor for the absence of the cow.

Following the definition of a delimiting factor—which states that when a simpler property is possible, one should not posit a more complex one—one accepts that the delimiting factor consists of a specific property that is pervasively distributed (*sakalaparyāpta*).

If it is argued: "How can delimitingness (*avacchedakatva*) be accepted? For even when that is not admitted, a cognition such as 'the pot exists' is possible," we say no. If delimitingness did not exist, then there would be no systematic determination of any of the relations between the sublated and the sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*) regarding cognitions qualified by absences.

And if that [distinction] were not established, all conventional transactions (*vyavahāra*) would be liable to collapse. For instance, in the case of a qualified cognition such as "the jar does not exist," if potness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth lacked the status of a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*), then by accepting the meaning to be merely the non-existence whose counter-positive is the jar, there would be no mutual distinction between the qualified cognitions: "the jar does not exist," "the blue jar does not exist," and "both the jar and the cloth do not exist. This is because in every case, there would be the same cognition of an absence whose counter-positive is the jar.

If, however, one accepts [the property of] being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*), then in the qualified cognition "a jar does not exist," there is the state of being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) determined by two delimiting factors residing solely in jar-ness; in the cognition "a blue jar does not exist," there is the state of being a counter-correlate determined by two delimiting factors residing in the two properties consisting of blueness and jar-ness; and in the cognition "neither a jar nor a cloth exists," [there is the state of being a counter-correlate determined by two delimiting factors residing in] jar-ness and cloth-ness.

This is because [the cognition] apprehends the state of being the counter-correlate of a delimitation residing in the three properties of bothness, substanceness, and potness. If it is argued that there is a difference in cognition due to a difference in the object, we say no; for in the cognition "the pot does not exist," there is the absence whose counter-correlate is the pot, whereas in the cognition "the blue pot does not exist," there is a difference between the two based on the difference of blueness, potness, and bothness. It is incorrect to claim that this difference in objects establishes a difference in the delimitations themselves.

If the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) is not accepted, then in cases such as "there is no jar by means of conjunction" (*saṃyogena ghaṭo nāsti*), the syntactic unity of the sentence would be impossible due to the impossibility of [the absence] being qualified [by that relation]. However, if the status of being a delimiting factor is accepted, then the meaning of "by means of conjunction" (*saṃyogena*) is "being delimited by the relation of conjunction. This [delimitation] is construed with the relation of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), and it is construed with the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) as being delimited by the relation of the delimiting factor of counter-positiveness; thus, [the absence is understood] through the relation of counter-positiveness delimited by the relation of conjunction.

"An absence possessing a jar," or "an absence possessing the nature of a jar (ghaṭatva) by way of the relation of a counter-correlativity delimited by the relation of delimited conjunction"—even if you do not wish it so, you must admit this delimiting factor (avacchedakatva). Let this elaborate discussion on delimiting factor as a specific kind of essential relation (svarūpasambandha) suffice; such is the view of the *Khaṇḍanapariśiṣṭa* text.

Now, if it is asked: "How is the existence of cognition (*jñāna*) accepted, while the existence of the object (*viṣaya*) is not accepted? If both are accepted on the basis of verbal testimony (*vākya*), then that [existence] is possible for both," we say no; because both affirmation (*vidhi*) and negation (*niṣedha*) are manifested by cognition. Otherwise, neither of the two would be established. Since their non-establishment would likewise follow [if cognition were denied], even against one's will, the existence of cognition must be accepted.

Furthermore, if, as in the case of a lamp or the sun, cognition illuminates its object, so too the object must likewise animate the cognition; since the arising of cognition is impossible without an object, the existence of the object must necessarily be admitted, because both are mutually dependent. Even so, since the fact that cognitions are all-pervasive is established by both parties, its validity is necessary; however, the object does not possess such [pervasive] existence, and therefore it lacks reality.

Furthermore, if falsity is accepted on the grounds of being an object (*viṣayatva*), then since cognition (*jñāna*) itself is also manifested by its own reflexive awareness (*svānuvyavasāya*), it too would incur the status of being an object; consequently, the falsity of cognition would be unavoidable. The reality of cognition has been clearly established in the *Bhāṣya* and other works. A detailed investigation regarding Gautama and others is to be found in the *Khaṇḍanapariśiṣṭa*.

In the sentence "Devadatta goes to the house" (*devadatto gṛhaṃ gacchati*), there are six words: *devadatta* (1), *su* (2), *gṛha* (3), *am* (4), *gam* (5), and *tip* (6). The word-meanings (*padārthas*) are as follows: 1. Devadatta-ness (*devadattatva*), 2. Devadatta, 3. Inherence (*samavāya*), 4. Masculinity (*puṃstvatva*), 5. Masculinity, 6. Inherence, 7. Oneness-ness (*ekatvattva*), 8. Oneness, 9. Inherence, 10. House-ness (*gṛhatva*), 11. House, 12. Inherence, 13. Neuter-ness (*klībattvatva*), 14. Neuter-ness, 15. Inherence, 16. Oneness-ness (*ekatvattva*), 17. Oneness, 18. Inherence, 19. Object-ness (*karmatva*), 20. Object (*karman*), 21. Inherence.

22. The state of being motion (gamanatva), 23. motion (gamana), 24. inherence (samavāya), 25. agency (kartṛtva), 26. the present tense (vartamānakāla), 27. the oneness residing in the agent (kartṛgataikatvatva), 28. oneness (ekatva), 29. inherence (samavāya), 30. the non-difference of Devadatta from the agent (devadattasya kartary abhedaḥ), and 33. the relationship of the object of action with the action of going for the referent of the other word (anyapadārthasya gamanakriyāyāṃ karmakriyābhāvasambandhaḥ).

The *yojanā* (synthetic unification) is that which is co-located with the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in Caitra—which is determined by a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) residing in "Caitra-ness" as delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), and which is also determined by a qualifierhood residing in "oneness" as delimited by the property of oneness (*ekatvatva*) and delimited by the relation of inherence—and which [qualifierhood] is itself determined by a qualifierhood residing in "Caitra-ness" as delimited by the relation of inherence. Furthermore, it is determined by a qualifierhood residing in Caitra, which is delimited by the relation of identity (*abheda*) and delimited by the property of "Caitra-ness."

The qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) residing in the agent, delimited by agency (kartṛtva) and determined by such a mode (prakāratā); the modehood (prakāratā) residing in the non-present time, delimited by the present time and determined by the relation of "being delimited" (paricchinnatva), which is itself determined by that [agent-]qualificandhood; the modehood residing in the house, delimited by houseness (gṛhatva) and determined by the relation of identity (abheda), which is itself determined by that [non-present-time-]modehood; and the qualificandhood residing in the object (karman), delimited by objecthood (karmatva), which is itself determined by that [house-]modehood.

The verbal cognition possesses a qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the action, which is delimited by the universal "action-ness" (kriyātva) and is determined by all the aforementioned qualifiers: namely, a qualifierness (prakāratā) residing in conjunction (saṃyoga), delimited by the universal "conjunction-ness" (saṃyogatva), related through the relation of "favorability" (anukūlatva), and co-located with a qualificandumness residing in the object; this latter qualificandumness resides in the object, is delimited by "object-ness" (karmatva), related through the relation of "inherence" (niṣṭhatva), and is co-located with a qualificandumness residing in the substratum [of the agent]. (Note: This sentence describes the structure of a complex verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) involving an action, its locus, and its result, specifically analyzing the relations between the properties and their respective loci.)

Regarding the statement "the pot is blue," according to Gautama’s sūtra—"The referent of a word consists of the genus (*jāti*), the configuration (*ākṛti*), and the individual (*vyakti*)"—the expressive power (*śakti*) of those respective words resides in the genus, the configuration, the inherence (*samavāya*), and the individual. Thus, there is a threefold delimitation (*avacchedakatā*)—pertaining to the knowledge of the function (*vṛtti*), the knowledge of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), and the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). In this case, these are: blueness (*nīlatva*), the inherence of blue, potness (*ghaṭatva*), the inherence of the pot, and non-difference (*abheda*).

The deliminatorhood residing in the deliminatorhood residing in the deliminatorhood residing in the deliminatorhood that is non-difference; the deliminatorhood residing in the deliminatorhood residing in the deliminatorhood residing in the relational objectivity residing in inherence, which is qualified by such [prior] deliminatorhood; the deliminatorhood residing in the deliminatorhood residing in the deliminatorhood residing in the deliminatorhood residing in blueness, which is qualified by such [prior] deliminatorhood; and the deliminatorhood residing in "blue" which is qualified by such [prior] deliminatorhood.

The verbal cognition is that which possesses a qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) residing in the jar, which is determined by a delimitorhood (avacchedakatā) residing in a delimitorhood residing in a delimitorhood residing in a relational objectivity (sāṃsargika-viṣayatā) residing in the inherence (samavāya) residing in the jar and the jar-ness; this [relational objectivity] is determined by a delimitorhood residing in a delimitorhood residing in a delimitorhood residing in the jar-ness; and this [jar-ness] is determined by a delimitorhood residing in a delimitorhood residing in a delimitorhood residing in such a delimitorhood.

The coarse meaning is: "The pot exists" means that existence resides in an agent non-different from the pot. Specifically, it refers to that which is the qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) residing in the pot, delimited by the property of potness, which is determined by a modehood (prakāratā) residing in oneness, delimited by the property of oneness, and delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya). Furthermore, it refers to that which is the qualificandhood residing in the agent, delimited by the property of agency, which is determined by a modehood residing in the pot, delimited by the property of potness, and delimited by the relation of identity (abheda), and which is co-located with such a qualificandhood.

The verbal cognition (śābdabodha) is that which possesses such a qualificandumhood (*viśeṣyatā*), namely: a qualificandumhood residing in existence (*sattā*)—delimited by the property of "existence-ness" (*sattātva*) and determined by a qualifierhood residing in the present time, which is itself delimited by the relation of "present-time-ness" and determined by a qualifierhood residing in the agent (*kartṛ*), which is delimited by the property of "agenthood" (*kartṛtva*) and determined by the relation of "subsistence" (*vṛttitva*), and which is co-located with such a qualificandumhood. Now, the meaning of the term "paryāpti" (pervasion/totality).
Paryāpti (collective inherence) is a specific type of essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) evidenced by such cognitions as "this is one jar" or "these are two.

The divine convention (*saṃketa*) regarding the word *puṣpavant* is precisely of the form: "Let there arise from the word *puṣpavant* a verbal cognition having as its object that which is delimited by both moonhood and sunhood. It should not be argued that because of a convention of the form "let there be a cognition having as its object only that which is delimited by moonhood from the word *puṣpavant*," there would also be a cognition of the moon alone [from that word].

The apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) has as its qualifier the property of having a scope-determining factor (*viṣayatāvacchedakatā*) that is pervasively present (*paryāpta*) in the state of being a cognition whose objects are delimited by candra-ness (moon-ness) produced by the word *puṣpavant* and whose object is delimited by sūrya-ness (sun-ness). Since the delimitor of the effect-nature (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is precisely the state of being a cognition whose qualifiers are both properties, there is not a single [unified] cognition; for, according to the aforementioned method, the relation of pervasive presence (*paryāpti*) is introduced [into the definition].

Is the being delimited by a relation present in the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) or in the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*)? For instance, in a cognition such as "the blue pot," is it one where the qualificandhood delimited by potness is characterized by a qualifierhood delimited by blueness and delimited by the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*), or rather is it one where the qualificandhood delimited by potness is characterized by a qualifierhood delimited by blueness and delimited by the relation of identity?

Due to parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more appropriate that the relation-restrictedness belongs to the qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) alone, and not to the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*). For instance, regarding the cognition "The jar does not exist by way of conjunction," the cognitions such as "The ground possesses a jar by way of conjunction," "The mountain possesses a jar by way of conjunction," and "The house possesses a jar by way of conjunction" act as inhibitors in one and the same form—namely, as cognitions possessing a qualifier-ness delimited by the relation of conjunction. Consequently, there is parsimony in their acting as inhibitors toward the cognition of the absence of that [jar] (i.e., the cognition "The jar does not exist by way of conjunction").

Nor should it be argued that the relation of sublation and sublation (pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva) should exist simply by virtue of being a certainty possessing a qualifierhood delimited by the universal "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).

This is because, since cognitions such as "the cloth possesses a pot through inherence" (*samavāyena ghaṭavān paṭaḥ*) would also result in being sublaters, the inclusion of the [specific] relation is necessary.

Nor should it be argued that the status of being a sublater exists simply by virtue of being a certainty possessing a qualificandumhood delimited by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as determined by a qualifierhood delimited by "pot-ness."
Otherwise, there would be no possibility of [the cognition] "the jar-possessor by way of conjunction" acting as an obstacle [to the inference].
Now, the question arises: what is this so-called "being determined" (*nirūpitatva*)?
It is the state of possessing a determinateness (*nirūpyatā*) that is itself determined by a determinerhood (*nirūpakatā*) residing in some locus whatsoever.
The nature of being a relatum (*nirūpakatva*) consists in possessing a relatumness that is itself determined by a determinateness (*niṣṭhanirūpyatā*) which is in turn determined by something else.

Now, one might object: since both the mode-ness (*prakāratā*) and the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) are categories that possess a relatum, what is the fault in not accepting that "the qualificand-ness determined by the mode-ness" is the same as "the mode-ness determined by the qualificand-ness"? If this were accepted, then regarding the cognition "the ground possesses the absence of a jar through conjunction," the certain knowledge "the ground possesses a jar through conjunction" would [obstruct it]. This is because they stand in a mutual relationship of the determined and the determiner (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*).

Just as there is an obstructive capacity (pratibandhakatva) by virtue of being a certainty (*niścaya*) whose qualificative mode (*prakāratā*) is delimited by potness (*ghaṭatva*) and related through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and whose qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) is delimited by earth-surface-ness (*bhūtalatva*), so too would there arise the unwanted consequence that a collective cognition (*samūhālambana-jñāna*) such as "the kitchen has a pot" and "the earth-surface has a pot"—being of the nature of such a certainty—would also possess obstructive capacity. However, the wise maintain that the relationship of mutual qualifier and qualified (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*) is accepted precisely because there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) [to prefer one over the other].

If it is argued that even when a jar exists, the expression "the jar is not" might be used because the absence of a jar from Prayāga exists here, [we reply: that is true; however, the word-meaning "jar" (ghaṭa) is construed with the meaning of the negative particle (nañ)—which is absence—by way of the relation of being the qualificand of a counter-correlativity delimited by itself (*svāvacchinnapratiyogitānirūpakatva*). This is because the cognition arises in the form: "an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*).
Now, [it is said]: "Similarity to that, absence, difference from that, and smallness of that..."
Non-praiseworthiness and contradiction—these six are proclaimed as the meanings of the negative particle (nañ). || 1 ||

Since it is well-established that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is indeed difference (*bheda*) based on such statements, it is more appropriate to maintain that in expressions such as "a non-blue pot" (*anīlo ghaṭaḥ*), the negative particle forming part of the compound indicates, by way of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), that which possesses difference, in order to account for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Objection: Let it be that in instances such as "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," "there is no jar on the ground," "the house possesses the absence of a jar," "there is no merit in the person," and "it is like the meaning of a non-element," the absence is simply the very nature of the locus (*adhikaraṇasvarūpa*). In this way, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be well-established, there would be no need for a separate cognition of the sentence-meaning as an absence, and there would be economy of thought (*lāghava*). Furthermore, the assumption of a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of [the word] "different" (*bhedavati*) would be pointless. Response: True. However, in cases such as "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," the relationship between the container and the contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) exists between the locus and the absence.

It could not [be so], because there would be identity between the absence (the contained) and its locus, the ground. For according to the analysis, if the category of the locus were one thing and the category of the absence were another, then the relation of container and contained would be established. However, in reality, in accordance with the authoritative cognition that "the jar does not exist in the absence of the jar," identity as a non-difference also serves as a regulator of the container-and-contained relation in certain cases. By the use of the phrase "in certain cases," it is not the case that "the jar is in the jar"; for this very reason, in the system of the Vedāntins—who maintain the non-difference of qualities and so forth from the substance—the cognition "color is in the jar" is successfully accounted for.

As it has been stated in the *Laghusiddhāntacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Advaitasiddhi*: "In cases such as 'color in the jar,' the relation of substratum-ship is accepted as being precisely identity (*tādātmya*) in the form of 'colorness' and so forth, rather than any other relation."

Nor should it be argued that, according to the rule that the individual instance (*vyakti*) perceived by a particular sense organ is grasped by that very same organ, as are its substrate (*āśraya*), its genus (*jāti*), and its absence (*abhāva*), there would be the impossibility of the nose-organ (*ghrāṇendriya*) not grasping [the absence of smell] in cases such as "there is no smell in water" or "water possesses the absence of smell," because the locus and the absence are identical; for this is so because the nose, tongue, and ear lack the capacity to grasp substances. [This is not so] because even though the water and the absence of smell are identical, the absence of smell whose nature is water...

Since there is no determining factor (*vinigamanā*) for the general property of being "the mere absence of smell devoid of water," the fact that it is perceivable by the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇendriya-grāhyatva*) remains unavoidable; therefore, if non-existence (*abhāva*) is of the nature of its locus (*adhikaraṇa-svarūpa*), there is no fault whatsoever, because this is a specific conceptualization (*viśiṣṭa-kalpanā*).

Nor should it be argued: "Why resort to a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for the negative particle (*nañ*) when it possesses a distinct meaning? Let there be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Since the difference is the meaning of the indeclinable (*nipāta*) and is also the meaning of the word forming the compound, there is no fault in its connection with the meaning of the noun through the relation of difference. Furthermore, since the rule that 'the direct connection between the meanings of two nominal stems—provided they are other than an indeclinable—or between the meanings of two nominal stems and a verb, provided they are other than an indeclinable, through the relation of difference is unestablished' does not apply here, there is no violation of that restriction. This cannot be maintained, for [otherwise] it would be like saying "the difference from blue in water."

In the case of *jale nīlam* ("blue in the water") as well, there ought to be a cognition of the relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*) between "blue" and its qualifier. Nor should it be said that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyavahāra*) of words denoting a qualificand and a qualifier with identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktika*) is the cause [of such a cognition]; for such a rule is accepted only for the cognition of identity. In fact, however, since there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*), the knowledge of the co-occurrence of words denoting a qualificand and a qualifier with identical case-endings is the cause for both the cognition of identity and the cognition of difference (*bhedānvaya*). Therefore, the question arises: one must consider the fault of the cognition of difference in the aforementioned usage, because otherwise it would be untenable.

According to the rule that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyavahāra*) of a word denoting the locus (*anuyogin*) in the locative case is the cause for the cognition of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) from the sentence "water is not non-blue" immediately after the cognition produced by the sentence "water is blue."

In the preceding sentence, because there is no word denoting the locus (*anuyogin*) ending in the locative case, there is no cognition of absolute non-existence; consequently, one must reluctantly accept that it is only the cognition of the difference from the difference from blue that is intended. Furthermore, since there is no contradiction between that [cognition] and the cognition of the difference from blue in water, the relationship of sublated and sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*) is untenable. However, if "difference" is taken as the secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*), then the resulting cognition—having the form "the difference from that which possesses the difference from blue"—prevents a cognition having the form "that which possesses the difference from blue" through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*); thus, there is no fault.

Furthermore, while it would be sufficient to say "the quality of blue exists in this [gem]," there is a rule that the word *tad* (that) does not refer to a single part [of a compound] when that part is presented through its own function (*vṛtti*), in order to prevent the word *tad* from referring to the object "blue. Consequently, in examples such as *anīlaṃ jalam* (the water is non-blue) or *so 'bhāvaḥ* (it is absence), since the negative particle *nañ* has the meaning of difference (*bheda*), and because [difference] is not a single part [of the compound], there is no secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for the possessor of difference; thus, it would follow that the word *tad* refers to the difference itself. However, if there were secondary signification for the possessor of difference, then because difference is a single part, it would not be referred to by the word *tad*.
In reality, however—

Where there is the causal complex for both a perception that apprehends the qualified presence (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of a difference from blue—having the form "water is a cognizable object distinct from that which possesses the difference from blue"—and a verbal cognition having the form "water is not blue," the opponent must postulate that the causal complex for the aforementioned verbal cognition acts as an inhibitor of the perception in order to exclude it; this constitutes a great complexity (*mahāgaurava*).
In reality, however:

Since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is pervaded by having the same gender, the absence of that [gender agreement] would entail the absence of its pervader; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of grammatical correctness even for such expressions as "water is not blue" (*jalam anīlam*). To avoid this consequence of grammatical correctness, one must accept a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "that which possesses difference" (*bhedavat*) in order to establish coreferentiality; thus, there is the status of being a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭatva*). In the case of "the ground is possessed of a jar" (*ghaṭavad bhūtalam*), the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) has as its qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) the groundness (*bhūtalatva*) delimited by the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*), which is itself determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) delimited by jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and restricted by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
"The ground is possessed of the absence of a jar.

[This cognition] is qualified by a qualifierhood delimited by the nature of absence (*abhāvatva*), which is itself delimited by an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*) and is determined by a qualifierhood delimited by the nature of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*), which is in turn delimited by a relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Furthermore, it is determined by a qualifierhood residing in the absence, which is non-different from the qualificandhood delimited by the nature of absence and itself delimited by an essential relation.

Furthermore, there arises a verbal cognition characterized by a qualificandumness delimited by "earth-surface-ness" (bhūtalatva), which is determined by a qualifierhood that is co-located with a qualificandumness delimited by "absence-ness" (abhāvatva)—the latter being determined by a qualifierhood delimited by "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) and qualified by a relation of conjunction (saṃyoga). This is the broad meaning.

The resulting verbal cognition is one characterized by a qualificandum-ness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the ground (bhūtala), which is itself determined by a delimitor-ness (avacchedakatā) residing in the ground; this delimitor-ness is non-limited (niravacchinna) and is delimited by the relation of identity (svarūpasambandha); furthermore, it is determined by a delimitor-ness residing in "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva), which is non-limited and is delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya) as qualified by the relation of conjunction (saṃyoga). This is the verbal cognition [arising from the sentence].

The qualificative-ness (viśeṣyatā) residing in absence (abhāva), which is determined by an unconditioned, non-limited delimitor-ship (avacchedakatā) residing in absentiality (abhāvatva) and delimited by the relation of self-linking (svarūpa-sambandha); this [absentiality] is determined by a qualifier-ness (prakāratā) delimited by the relation of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitva); this [counter-correlativity] is determined by a qualifier-ness residing in the jar (ghaṭa) and determined by such a delimitor-ship; this [delimitor-ship] is a non-limited, non-delimiting factor residing in jar-ness (ghaṭatva) and delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya) as conditioned by the relation of conjunction (saṃyoga).

The verbal cognition is one characterized by a qualificandum-ness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the ground, which is itself determined by a qualifier-ness (prakāratā) that resides in the same locus as such a qualificandum-ness and is delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya), and this qualifier-ness has an unconditioned non-limiting factor (niravacchinnāvacchedakatā) residing in "ground-ness" (bhūtalatva). Alternatively, the cognition is the opposite:
"the ground possesses the absence of a jar."

That which is delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya-sambandha) and is an undelimited delimitorhood (niravacchinna-avacchedakatā) residing in the earth-surface; that which is the qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the earth-surface as determined by such a delimitorhood; that which is the modehood (prakāratā) residing in absence (abhāva), delimited by its own nature (svarūpa-sambandha) and delimited by [the absence itself], as determined by such a qualificandumness; and that which is delimited by the modehood residing in absence, as determined by the relation of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitva-sambandha). It is delimited by such a modehood.

It is a verbal cognition characterized by a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) residing in a jar, which is itself defined by a non-restricted delimitationhood (*anavacchedakatā*) residing in "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), this delimitationhood being delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), and this delimitationhood being defined by a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), which is either non-different from or co-referential with that [absence]. In the case of "There is no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭo nāsti*) and "The jar does not exist on the ground" (*ghaṭo nāsti bhūtale*),

the relation of qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*) pertains to the objective scope (*vidheyatā*) termed "subjecthood" (*uddeśyatva*), while the relation of qualifierhood (*prakāratā-sambandha*) pertains to the objective scope termed "predicability" (*vidheyatva*).

"The mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*); "fire is on the mountain" (*parvate vahniḥ*); "the mountain is the locusness (*uddeśyatā*), and fire is the predicate-ness (*vidheyatā*). In the rule "an *iK* vowel becomes *yaṇ* before an *aC* vowel" (*iko yaṇaci*), there is a relation of qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) with respect to the locusness residing in the *iK*, and a relation of mode-ness (*prakāratā*) with respect to the predicate-ness residing in the *yaṇ*. "A jar is the agent of existence that lacks occurrence as determined by the ground" (*bhūtalanirūpitavṛttitvābhāvavatsattākarttako ghaṭaḥ*); "existence is the agent of a jar that lacks occurrence as determined by the ground" (*bhūtalanirūpitavṛttitvābhāvavadghaṭakartṛkā sattā*). The absence of "existence as the agent of a jar possessing occurrence as determined by the ground" (*bhūtalanirūpitavṛttitvavaddhaṭakartṛkasattābhāvaḥ*) is the absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is "existence as the agent of a jar possessing occurrence as determined by the ground."
In reality, however, "there is a pot on the ground" means:
the pot possesses a subsistence as determined by the ground;

the cognition is that the counter-positive, which is the pot possessing subsistence as determined by the ground, has the absence as its relatum (anuyogin); thus, the referent of the word "pot" is construed with the absence through the relation of being the relatum (anuyogitā).

The qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the ground, which is determined by a qualifier-ness (prakāratā) delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya) as it resides in the nature of being ground; [the qualifier-ness] which is non-different from such a qualificand-ness, or delimited by the nature of being a qualificand-ness, or co-referential with such a qualificand-ness; [the qualifier-ness] residing in the meaning of the locative case, delimited by the nature of being "residing-ness" and delimited by the relation of identity (svarūpa-sambandha); [the qualifier-ness] determined by such a qualifier-ness; [the qualifier-ness] residing in the absence (abhāva), delimited by the nature of being an absence.

The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) possesses a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) residing in "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), which is unconditioned (*niravacchinna*) and delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). This qualifierhood is defined by a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). This qualificandhood is either identical to or co-referential with that which delimits it; such [qualificandhood] is a qualificandhood residing in an absence (*abhāva*), which is either identical to or co-referential with that which delimits it—the qualificandhood being delimited by such a subjecthood (*viśeṣyatva*). Such a subjecthood is delimited by the subjecthood of "that" (the pot), which is non-different from or co-referential with it. Thus, the sentence "There is no pot on the ground" (*ghaṭo nāsti bhūtale*) results in the following verbal cognition: [The cognition is] qualified by a qualifierhood residing in "pot-ness," which is unconditioned and delimited by the relation of inherence. This qualifierhood is defined by a qualificandhood residing in the counter-correlative. This qualificandhood is either identical to or co-referential with that which delimits it; such [qualificandhood] is a qualificandhood residing in an absence, which is either identical to or co-referential with that which delimits it—the qualificandhood being delimited by such a subjecthood. Such a subjecthood is delimited by the subjecthood of "that" (the pot), which is non-different from or co-referential with it. Thus, the sentence "There is no pot on the ground" results in the aforementioned verbal cognition.

That which is the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in a jar, which is determined by an unconditioned mode-ness (*niravacchinnaprakāratā*) residing in "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*); that which is the mode-ness residing in a jar, which is co-located with such a qualificand-ness, delimited by such a qualificand-ness, or non-different from such a qualificand-ness; that which is the qualificand-ness delimited by the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitvasambandha*), which is co-located with such a mode-ness; and that which is determined by such a mode-ness... [the sentence continues].

The qualificative-ness (viśeṣyatā) residing in absence, which is delimited by the state of being an absence delimited by the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*); or that which is delimited by such qualificative-ness, or non-different from it; the qualificative-ness residing in absence; the qualificative-ness residing in the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) related by the relation of counter-correlativity, which is itself determined by such [prior] qualificative-ness; the qualificative-ness residing in the state of occurring in the locative case-meaning, which is delimited by the state of being "occurring in the locative case-meaning" and related by the relation of identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*); the qualificative-ness which is co-locational with such a qualificative-ness; and that [cognition] which is determined by such a qualificative-ness...

The subtle meaning is as follows: the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) possesses such a mode (prakāratā) which is itself determined by a qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the locus (bhūtala). It is held that an exposition (vyākhyāna) is sixfold: (1) the determination of the subject matter (pakṣaccheda), (2) the statement of the word-meanings (padārthokti), (3) the analysis of the compound (vigraha), (4) the syntactical connection (vākyayojanā), (5) the anticipation of objections (ākṣepa), and (6) the resolution [of those objections] (samādhāna).
A sentence is of two kinds:

that which intends the connection of the predicate with the delimitor of the subjecthood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), and that which intends the connection of the predicate with what is co-locatable (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the delimitor of the subjecthood. To illustrate:

The conch of the Lord of Lakṣmī is Pāñcajanya, and the discus is Sudarśana. The intended meaning (*tātparya*) is the connection of the word "Pāñcajanya" with the denotable object (*śakyārtha*) as delimited by the property of being a conch related to Viṣṇu. The mind (*manas*) is formless and possesses touch. The intended meaning is the connection of the word "mind" with the denotable object through the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the state of possessing touch qualified by the absence of form. This is because the universal (*jāti*) "mind-ness" (*manastva*) alone is the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). The state of possessing touch qualified by the absence of form also exists in air, ether, and so forth; therefore, the connection occurs only by way of co-occurrence, and not by way of the relation between the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*).

Now, in the context of investigating which position is superior—given that some accept a relation of the nature of the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) between the qualifierhood and the qualificandhood residing in the same locus, while others maintain a relation of identity (*abheda*) between them—it appears that the relation of the delimited and the delimiter is indeed the most appropriate.

For instance, if an identity relation (*abheda-sambandha*) is postulated between those two, then just as a certainty characterized by a qualificandumness delimited by stick-ness, which is determined by a qualifierhood delimited by person-ness and restricted by the relation of conjunction—as in the cognition "the stick possesses the absence of a person through conjunction"—is an inhibitor with respect to the cognition "the stick possesses a person through conjunction," so too is the certainty "this [person] possesses a red-stick-person" an inhibitor.

By virtue of possessing the nature of an obstructive factor (pratibandhakatā), which consists in being a certainty characterized by a qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā) delimited by stickness (daṇḍatva), as determined by a subjectness (prakāratā) delimited by personhood (puruṣatva) and delimited by a relation of conjunction (saṃyoga).

It would result in being an obstructive factor (*pratibandhakatva*). This is because it is logical that such a defect—namely, the consequence of being an obstructive factor—would arise, due to the identity between: (1) the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the person, which is determined by the qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in the staff; and (2) the qualifier-ness residing in the person, which is determined by the qualificand-ness residing in the location; both of these [latter two] being identical with the qualificand-ness residing in the staff, which is determined by the qualifier-ness residing in the red [color], and the qualifier-ness residing in the location, respectively.

The point is that if one accepts the relation of the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*), then no fault can arise because of the difference between the delimiters. Now, an objection is raised: in the aforementioned cognitions, it is heard everywhere without any decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*) whether the objectness (*viśeṣyatā*) is qualified by a modehood (*prakāratā*) delimited by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or rather by the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa*). Therefore, the question arises as to how one should establish with proof whether this "being delimited by a relation" should be introduced into the objectness or into the modehood.

To this it is replied: the property of being delimited by a relation (*sambandhāvacchinnatva*) is to be included in the qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) alone, and not in the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*). For instance, with respect to the cognition "the pot does not reside in the ground by way of conjunction" (*saṃyogena ghaṭo na vṛttaḥ*), the certainty-cognitions such as "the ground possesses the pot by way of conjunction," "the mountain possesses the pot by way of conjunction," and "the cloth possesses the pot by way of conjunction," function as inhibitors in a single uniform manner—namely, by virtue of being certainty-cognitions whose qualifier-ness is delimited by the relation of conjunction. Thus, there is the possibility of parsimony (*lāghava*).

[Objection: Even so, let the various determinate cognitions (*niścaya*) of a jar have their status as obstructors (*pratibandhakatva*) by means of one and the same recurring form; however, because there is no further purpose, the inclusion of "being delimited by a relation" (*sambandhāvacchinnatva*) within that delimiting qualifier-ness (*avacchedaka-prakāratā*) is indeed useless. [Reply: No, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the cognition "the cloth possesses a jar by way of inherence" (*samavāyena ghaṭavān paṭaḥ*) would be an obstructor. This is because it is impossible for such a cognition to be an obstructor by virtue of being a determination possessing a qualifier-ness delimited by "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatvāvacchinna-prakāratā*).

It should not be argued that since the property of being delimited by a relation (*sambandhāvacchinnatva*) is abandoned in the case of the mode (*prakāratā*) and accepted only in the case of the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*), the fault of over-extension—whereby the cognition "the cloth has a pot by way of inherence" would result in being a sublater (*pratibandhaka*) even when sublateness is defined [in terms of the mode]—is avoided; for [sublateness] consists in being a certainty (*niścaya*) possessing a qualificandumness delimited by a relation, which is itself delimited by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as determined by a mode delimited by pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*).

For there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence that the cognition "the locus possesses a jar by way of conjunction" (*saṃyogena ghaṭavān*)—which is "pure," meaning its qualificandum is not cognized as being delimited by any [specific relation]—would not function as an obstacle [to the arising of a contrary cognition]. Furthermore, there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) due to the infinity of those various non-delimited qualificanda. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the property of being delimited by a relation should be introduced only into the "mode-ness" (*prakāratā*), and not into the "qualificandum-ness" (*viśeṣyatā*).

If it is asked: "How can the relationship of mutual definition (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*) be accepted between the qualifier-nature (*prakāratā*) and the qualificand-nature (*viśeṣyatā*), between the produced and the producer, between the contained and the container, and between the delimited and the delimiter? We reply: "It is for the sake of establishing the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*prativadhya-pratibandhakabhāva*) in its true nature."

Otherwise, if the relationship between the determined (*nirūpya*) and the determiner (*nirūpaka*) is not accepted, then with respect to the cognition "the ground possesses the absence of a jar by way of conjunction" (*saṃyogena ghaṭābhāvavad bhūtalam*), which is a knowledge characterized by a subjecthood delimited by the nature of the ground (*bhūtalatva*) and a qualificandumhood delimited by a modehood delimited by the nature of the absence of a jar as qualified by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sambandhāvacchinnaghaṭābhāvatvāvacchinnaprakāratākabhūtalattvāvacchinnaviśeṣyatākajñāna*), [the counter-cognition] "the ground possesses a jar by way of conjunction" (*saṃyogena ghaṭavad bhūtalam*), which is a certainty characterized by a subjecthood delimited by the nature of the ground and a modehood delimited by the nature of the jar as qualified by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sambandhāvacchinnaghaṭatvāvacchinnaprakāratākabhūtalattvāvacchinnaviśeṣyatākaniścayatvena*), would function as an inhibitor.

Otherwise, even a collective cognition (*samūhālambana-jñāna*) such as "the kitchen is like a pot; the floor is like a cloth" would result in being an obstacle to [the inference], by virtue of being a certainty (*niścaya*) of that same kind. However, if one accepts a mutual relationship of the defined (*nirūpya*) and the definer (*nirūpaka*), then it is possible to avoid this [undesired consequence] simply through the difference in the definers. The truth is that this relationship of the defined and the definer is understood precisely because there is no other determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*).

Furthermore, a relation that does not regulate the occurrence of a property (*vṛttyaniyāmaka-sambandha*) cannot be the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence (*abhāva*).

The status of being a locus-determiner (*adhikaraṇatāniyāmaka*) belongs only to such things as the substratum (*āśrayatva*), essential nature (*svarūpa*), and conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and it is precisely this that constitutes the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) of an absence. In the case of "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), since the relation of being-qualified-by (*nirūpitatva*) does not function as a locus-determiner with respect to the ownership (*svattva*) expressed by the genitive case, it does not serve as the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of the absence in expressions such as "the man is not the king's" (*na rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*).

By whatever relation a given object exists in a particular locus, by that very same relation the absence of that object in that very locus is also conveyed by the negative particle (*nañ*). However, it is impossible for any object, such as a king, to reside in a person by way of the relation of ownership (*svatva*), such that ownership would function as a determinant of occurrence (*vṛttiniyāmaka*). When one says "the king's man," the residence of the king in the man by way of the relation of ownership is not perceived in any way whatsoever, which would otherwise allow ownership to serve as a determinant of occurrence.

Furthermore, because ownership lacks the status of being a restrictor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) due to its not being a regulator of occurrence (*vṛttiniyāmakatva*), and because an absence whose counter-correlativity is restricted by the relation of ownership is not established anywhere, when the sentence "The man is not the king's" is uttered, an absence of the king whose counter-correlativity is restricted by the relation of ownership does not indeed become the object of cognition; rather, it is simply the absence of the king's ownership [that is cognized]. Therefore, the intention is that ownership possesses only the status of a qualifier (*prakāratva*) and not the status of a relation (*saṃsargatva*).

If it is asked: "How can the meaning of *vṛttyaniyāmaka* be 'that which lacks the status of being a determiner of locus (*adhikaraṇatāniyāmaka*)'?"—[the answer is as follows]: *Vṛtti* is the act of abiding (*vartanam*). The suffix *ktin* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) according to the rule *striyāṃ ktin*. Thus, *vṛtti* means "abiding" or "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, by the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (variously) in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *ktin* is also used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), as in the derivation of the word *vṛtti* from the sense "that in which things abide" (*vartante padārthā yasmin*). Therefore, the meaning of *vṛtti* here is "locus. Consequently, *vṛttyaniyāmaka* means "that which is not a determiner of locus."

That very relation which determines the relationship between locus and located—such as conjunction in the case of "the ground possesses a jar"—is itself the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of absence; however, this is not the case for relations such as "being characterized by" (*nirūpitatva*) in expressions like "the man is not [related] to the king," because of the description of the previously stated intention.

In reality, however, even for the owner of earrings and so forth, when the earrings are joined [to him], the cognition "Devadatta is earring-possessing" (*kuṇḍalī*) does not arise; therefore, even a relation that is not a determinant of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*) can indeed be the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence. Thus, [the cognition] "Devadatta is earring-possessing" does not occur. Furthermore, it should be understood that in cases such as "The substance goes, [but] non-existence does not," since a substratumhood delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), the cognition of its absence is impossible.
The question remains whether an absence whose counter-correlative is unestablished should be admitted or not.

Because non-existence (*abhāva*) is eternally dependent upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), non-existence has some specific counter-correlate; it is not devoid of a counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*). For if one were to say "there is no non-existence," there would arise the expectation—"What is not there? Of what is there non-existence?"—since such an inquiry necessarily falls within the scope of a specific cognition. Just as knowledge does not exist without an object but is always possessed of an object (*saviṣayaka*), so too non-existence is always possessed of a counter-correlate (*sapratiyogika*).

In such cases as "Caitra sees the jar," the seeing of a jar having Caitra as its agent is well-known; therefore, in instances such as "Caitra does not see the jar," the absence [of that action] is established because its counter-positive (the action) is well-known.

In expressions such as "The pot does not see space," "Non-existence does not see space," "Caitra smells space," "Space is not seen by Caitra," and "Caitra does not see space," [the negation *nañ*] is absent in the corresponding affirmative forms like "Caitra sees space. Since an action of seeing where Caitra is the agent and space is the object is not established [as a fact], there is no establishment of its absence (*abhāva*) anywhere; therefore, such negative usages do not occur, because their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are unestablished.

Those who follow the logical principles maintain that only for that counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) which is well-known in the world as existing independently can there occur usages such as "he does not see" (*na paśyati*), because of the connection with the aspect of non-existence (*abhāvāṃśa*) of that very thing; since smelling space (*ākāśa*) as an object is not known anywhere in the world, such usages as "he smells space" (*ākāśaṃ jighrati*) do not occur. In reality, however, in all cases, non-existence has only an unestablished counter-positive.

If, in such cases as "there is no jar on this ground," there is no established instance whatsoever of existence (sattā) caused by a jar delimited by this particular location, how can there be a cognition of the absence of that existence which has [the jar] as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)? This is the underlying point: in expressions such as "there is no jar on this ground," since the ground is more extensive than the jar and possesses a larger magnitude, it is well-established that the existence of the jar does not occur delimited by any part of the entire ground.

It is well known to all that even when a jar exists on the ground in a particular location, there is an absence of the jar with respect to the entire ground. This is because, in relation to the ground, the jar is of a smaller dimension; thus, it is understood by common experience that its existence is possible only within the limitation of a small area. There are many such locations on the ground where the presence of a jar is possible, yet they have never come within the range of hearing or sight due to a lack of necessity.

Just as in the case of a mountain cave, a portion of the ocean, or the ground within the middle of a house wall, the existence of a jar never occurs in these places; it is with this intention that one says, "There is no jar here. When it is uttered, "There is no jar on this ground," the existence of a jar—performed by the agent [the jar]—is entirely unestablished with respect to this specific location delimited by the surface of the earth.

And thus, one might ask: "Are there not many such absences whose counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are unestablished in these types of cases? It must be said that no deliberation can be made between absences with established counter-correlates and absences with unestablished counter-correlates; rather, based on the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), the cognition has as its object the absence of this or that specific counter-correlate in a general form. The inquiry as to whether the counter-correlate is established or unestablished is not a matter accepted by all traditions—enough of this. Furthermore, the word "one" (*eka*) signifies both oneness (*ekatva*) and the property of residing in only one thing (*ekamātravṛttitva*).
The word *eka* is employed in the sense of "alone," "principal," "first," and likewise "exclusive"; it is also used for "common," "equal," "small," and "number. (1)
