Thus, both [the noun and the suffix] are expressed. In the expression "the rice is ready" (*sampanno vrīhiḥ*), the meaning of the *su*-suffix is not merely oneness as a number; rather, the usage of "the rice is ready" is intended to convey the sense that "the rice itself has become ready, and not some other food."

If one accepts that the meaning of the singular number is merely oneness (*ekatvamātra*), then the speaker’s intended exclusion of the "ripening" found in other grains would not be established. This is because, while something distinct from rice—such as another food—that belongs to the same genus as rice, is planted in a field immediately adjacent to the field where the rice seeds were sown at the very time of sowing, and serves as the locus of the activity conducive to its planting, it lacks ripening in relation to rice; rather, ripening occurs only in the rice itself. Thus, the exclusion of ripening in other grains would not be achieved. However, [this is achieved by the definition provided].

The meaning of the singular number is precisely that state of being devoid of a second of the same class, which consists in the singularity that is not a delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in something of its own class. The method for excluding others is as follows.

In a place where there are many jars, there is a yellow jar (*pītaghaṭa*) and a second blue jar (*nīlaghaṭa*) belonging to its same class (*sajātīya*). In that blue jar, the difference from the yellow jar (*pītaghaṭabheda*) certainly exists; and since the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of that difference is the yellow jar, the oneness (*ekatva*) residing therein is precisely the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of that difference. Thus, that oneness consists in being devoid of a second [entity] of the same class. Therefore, in such a case, the plural number alone is logical. However, when only a single jar exists there, then...

Because there is no second pot of the same class, the oneness residing in the single present pot is precisely the non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the difference residing in a second pot of its own class. Thus, the meaning of the singular number is precisely this state of being a non-delimiter, which is the very nature of the singular case-ending. An example is: "The rice has ripened," and so forth.

In this context, if at some time there is another food distinct from rice (*vrīhi*), then because there exists another thing of the same class as rice by virtue of its being "ripe" (*sampanna*), the rice-ness (*vrīhitva*) residing in that [rice] is indeed the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of the difference existing therein [in the rice] with respect to that other rice. And when there is no other food intended for that purpose because it is not ripe, then since there is an absolute absence of anything of the same class as rice by way of its being "ripe," the rice-ness residing in the rice becomes precisely the non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of the difference residing in a second thing of its own class; that very state is what constitutes being devoid of a second thing of the same class.

For this very reason, in such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta svargakāma*), since the oneness residing in the animal—consisting in its being devoid of a second of the same class—is accepted, the accomplishment of *dharma* results from a sacrifice performed with a single animal. The manner of this coordination is as follows: one's own animal has a second animal of the same class; if that second animal were present at the sacrifice, then the difference from this [one's own] animal, which resides in that second animal, would be the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) for the oneness residing in this [one's own] animal.

If there is no second animal in the sacrifice, then this oneness residing in the animal is precisely the non-limiting condition of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of the difference residing in other animals of the same class; that itself is the state of being devoid of a second of the same class.

It should not be argued that, by accepting a non-dual homogeneity (*sājātya*) based on the property of being related to a sacrifice, this same distinction would apply even to ghee and other substances related to a sacrifice—such as when an animal is bound by someone on a sacrificial ground for the accomplishment of some other purpose—because there too, due to its being of the same genus as an animal, it would be unavoidable for it to serve as the delimitor of the counter-correlate of the difference (*bhedapratiyogitāvacchedakatva*). This is because we rely upon a homogeneity defined as "possessing the delimitor of the primary meaning (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*) as qualified by being related to the object denoted by the word co-occurrent with itself."

In the expression "svaṃ yajeta" (one should sacrifice one's own), the meaning is as follows: the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in its present tense form, when co-occurring with the word "self" (*sva*), refers to the meaning of the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*). This is qualified by the property of being related to that [sacrifice], which is co-referential with the relation to the sacrifice. That which serves as the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*)—namely, the generic property of "being a beast" (*paśutva*)—is the result. The point is this: in the case of a beast mentioned for the sake of another ritual action, there is no relation to the sacrifice; and in the case of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and so forth, there is no being delimited by the generic property of "beast-hood. Thus, in all such instances, this is the way to understand the meaning of the singular number. This is the general direction. Now, the question arises: what are *prakāratā* (the mode of presentation) and *viśeṣyatā* (the state of being the qualificandum)?

Being the state of being determined by a relation that is itself determined by qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) is "qualificative-ness" (*prakāratva*). Being the state of being determined by a relation that is itself determined by qualificative-ness is "qualificandness" (*viśeṣyatva*). Nor should it be argued that there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*), because the two—qualificative-ness and qualificandness—are related as the determiner and the determined (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*), such that the establishment of one cannot occur without the knowledge of the other. This is because, according to an undisputed principle, qualificative-ness is simply a particular kind of objecthood (*viṣayatā*), and qualificandness is likewise a particular kind of objecthood. Now, what is the question regarding "categorialness" (*padārthatva*)?

The definition of being a word-meaning (*padārthatva*) is: "being the relatum of a power residing in a specific word. It should not be argued that there is a logical fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) because the word "word" (*pada*) is employed in the definition in a general sense, and thus a cloth would be the meaning of the word "pot," and a pot would be the meaning of the word "cloth. This is not the case, because the definition is intended as "being the relatum of a power residing in a specific word [X]," where it is stated that a specific word [X] has the power to denote an object delimited by a property desired to be known by the speaker, which is characterized by being the object of a particular cognition. Thus, there is no flaw.

Nor is there a cognition consisting of a collective reference (*samūhālambana*) such as "the pot, the cloth, and the hut. Cognition is threefold: determinate (*savikalpaka*), indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*), and that which consists of a collective reference. In that case, regarding the cognition consisting of a collective reference mentioned here, must it not be said that one word would have another word as its meaning? [The answer is: It is the delimitingness (*avacchedakatā*), delimited by the relation of being the counter-correlative (*nirūpakatva*), which is defined by the producedness (*janyatā*) corresponding to the generative capacity (*janakatā*) delimited by the state of being a cognition whose object is the function (*vṛtti*) dependent upon the knowledge of the function residing in each respective word.

There is no defect in any respect regarding the definition of the referent (*padārtha*) according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), which states: "The state of being a referent consists in being the substratum of a cognitive objecthood (*viṣayatā*) that possesses such a delimitedness (*avacchedyatā*), where said delimitedness is itself determined by a delimitorhood (*avacchedakatā*) of that kind.

Now, an objection may be raised: if the word *tat* (that) is included [in the definition], there would be a lack of uniformity (*ananugama*) in the definition. If it were to have a general meaning, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of cognizing even an object that was perceived at one time as being the object of a cognition occurring at another time.

Furthermore, if it is argued that [the term] is the object of another person’s cognition and the verbal cognition of that other person, and thus, upon introducing the qualification "belonging to the specific time conducive to its own utterance," there is a total lack of uniformity because the word "own" (sva) refers to each individual instance, [we reply: no; one must accept a convention where the qualificandum of the cognition is of the form "let there be a cognition qualified by that word. And this being-qualified-by-that is [defined] by two relations: (1) having as its object that which is delimited by the delimitor of the objecthood in the cognition conducive to its own utterance, and (2) being produced by itself (svajanyatva).

The denotative function (*saṅketa*) of words such as *tat* (that) and so forth consists specifically in their particular word-sequence (*padānupūrvī*), which takes the form of the letter *ta* followed by the letter *ta*. Since this sequence is of a uniform nature across all instances of the word *tat*, there is no difference in the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word based on differences in individual word-manifestations (*padavyakti*). Furthermore, the word *tat* is fourfold, according to the distinctions of referring to an object that is about to be introduced (*prakramyamāṇa*), one already introduced (*prakrānta*), one well-known (*prasiddha*), or one previously experienced (*anubhūta*). Examples are: "Bring that which is here" (*tam ānaya ya iha asti*); "Bring that jar which is here" (*ghaṭa iha asti tam ānaya*); and "In his pure lineage" (*tad-anvaye śuddhimati*).

The referent of the word *indu* (moon) is the object of the term *kiṃ* (what/which); the referent of the word *mukha* (face) is the object of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). Through the relation of being a qualifier delimited by the relation of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*), the referent of the word *indu* is construed with the possibility denoted by the term *kiṃ*. Furthermore, that possibility is construed with the face through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). The resulting verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is: "The face is the locus of the possibility which possesses a qualifierhood characterized by a qualifierhood residing in the moon."

The intended meaning is that where there is a qualificandness (viśeṣyatā) determined by a qualifierhood (prakāratā) residing in some [object], and a qualifierhood determined by a qualificandness residing in that same [object]—that is to say, where the qualificandness is determined by the referent of one word and the qualifierhood is determined by the referent of another word—it is precisely in such a case that there is the relation of being a qualifier (prakāritā-sambandha). Causality (janakatva) is the state of being a cause (kāraṇatva).

And that [capacity] is of two kinds: essential fitness (*svarūpayogyatva*) and the state of being productive of a result (*phalopadhāyakatva*). Essential fitness consists in possessing the property that delimits causal status (*kāraṇatāvacchedakadharma*). For example, even a staff standing in a forest has causality with respect to a jar. The second kind is as follows: "Desire must be produced by knowledge; effort (*kṛti*) must be produced by desire; indeed, effort is produced by an operation (*vyāpāra*), and that which is produced by it is called the result. (Verse 1)

Kevalānvayitva (the state of being purely positive) is the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). A property that exists everywhere and whose absolute non-existence is unestablished is a purely positive property (*kevalānvayī*). For example, in the inference "The pot is denotable because it is cognizable," the property of cognizability (*prameyatva*) is purely positive. Gamakatva (the state of being a prover) is the state of having a constant expectancy (*nityasākāṅkṣatva*). In cases such as "Caitra’s teacher’s family" (*caitrasya gurukulam*) or "Caitra’s servant’s master" (*caitrasya dāsamārya*), although there is mutual dependence, a compound is formed because there is constant expectancy. Prāgabhāvatva (the state of being prior non-existence) is the state of being an entity that is subject to destruction.

Thus say the Naiyāyikas. The Grammarians (Śābdikas), however, maintain that prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is the subsistence of a cause in the form of potentiality (śakti). The Sāṅkhya teachers, on the other hand, assert that prior non-existence is simply the future state of an entity. The practical conclusion is that prior non-existence must be admitted in order to prevent the re-emergence of an already produced object, such as a jar, since its causes would still be present. Regarding expressions such as "the jar will be," there arises an inquiry as to which of the two—the base (prakṛti) or the suffix (pratyaya)—expresses prior non-existence. Furthermore, there is the matter of identity (tādātmya).

Some Vedāntins maintain that identity (*tādātmya*) is non-difference capable of tolerating difference. The proponents of Māyā (*māyāvādins*) hold that identity is the absence of having an existence distinct from the existence of that [other thing].
The Sāṅkhya teachers maintain that identity is a specific kind of relation that governs the cognitions of both difference and non-difference.
Some hold that identity is oneness (*aikya*). It is "that-ness" (*tadātman*); the state of being that is identity (*tādātmya*).

Having the same object (*samānaviṣayakatva*) means either possessing the quality of having a common substantive and qualifier in an identical form, or having as its object that which is the object of the other.
Thus, the two certainties—"The mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*) and "The mountain possesses the fire belonging to the kitchen" (*parvato mahānasīyavahnimān*)—have the same object.

Furthermore, being an "exciter" (*uttejakatva*) means being the counter-positive of an absence that has entered into the category of the obstructer (*pratibandhaka*). That a specific jewel (*maṇi*) is an obstructer with respect to burning is known through worldly experience.
Those learned in the treatises on poetics (*kāvyashāstra*), however, say that "incitement" (*prerakatva*) is "stimulation" (*uttejakatva*).
Some say that "stimulation" (*uttejakatva*) is "excitation" (*uddīpakatva*). Others say that "stimulation" (*uttejakatva*) is "augmentation" (*vardhakattva*). Thus he asks.

The word [is] dependent on an activity whose purpose is the desire to know (jijñāsā) and knowledge; for example, it is the meaning of the root *pṛcchati* in such expressions as "he asks the teacher about dharma."

In this context, the relation of "being the locus" (*guruvṛttitva*) is construed with the cognition that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root *pṛcchati* (to ask), while the relation of "having as its object a property" (*dharmaviṣayakatva*) is construed with the word [the utterance]. The objecthood (*viṣayatā*) of the word is connected to the operation (*vyāpāra*), and the objecthood of the cognition is also connected to the operation; since the cognition is indirectly a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root—which consists of the word—the teacher, who is the substratum of that [cognition], possesses the status of a secondary object (*gauṇakarmatā*), whereas the property, which is the object of the meaning of the verbal root, possesses the status of the primary object (*pradhānakarmatā*).

Some grammarians, however, say that [the root *pracch*] signifies an activity conducive to knowledge regarding the object of inquiry (*jijñāsā*). This [activity] consists of such things as the desire [expressed in the thought], "How should dharma be practiced? In examples such as "The disciple asks the teacher about dharma," they state that this is the meaning of the root *pracch*. Those learned in poetry say that *pracch* means "questioning. From the root *iccha*, by applying the suffix *aṅ* according to the rule "from roots ending in *ṣit* or from *bhid* etc., the suffix *aṅ* [is applied]," there occurs vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), resulting in *pṛccha*. From that, by adding the causative suffix *ṇic* and then the suffix *ṇvul*, one obtains *pṛcchaka* (one who asks). Thus, the abstract noun *praśnatva* is derived from *praśna*.

When, from a question-sentence, a relation of a thing qualified by a certain property (Dharma A) with a thing delimited by another property (Dharma B) is understood, and from the answer-sentence, a relation of that same thing qualified by Dharma A with a thing delimited by a property pervaded by Dharma B is understood, only then does the relationship of question and answer obtain. For example, to the question "From what [cause] is the jar? the answer is "The jar is from a staff. To the question "What does he do?", which concerns one qualified by effort, the answer "He cooks" conveys the understanding of the effort of cooking.

In a question, that which is primary—such as gender and number—precisely by means of that [correspondence] is what satisfies the desire to know regarding the object of the question. For instance, in response to the question "Who are his disciples?", the answer is "The Kaṭhas," and not "Kaṭha."

The nature of a question (*praśnatva*) consists in the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) regarding the name, purpose, and so forth [of the person addressed]. For example: "O sir, what is your name? For what purpose have you come here? In this context, by the word *jijñāsā*, there is indicated an activity conducive to the expression of that [desire]; furthermore, a question is defined as a request concerning something unknown. Moreover, the nature of a question is the manifestation of a desire to know, as in the question: "What is a *gavaya* like?"

Those who consider themselves experts in grammar (śābdikammanya), however, say that a question is the desire that prompts a subsequent [utterance]. Regarding this, the *Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya* states: "The word 'question' (praśna) signifies an activity conducive to the cognition of an object not yet known. If one did not possess a cognition regarding that object, the desire itself would not arise.
Desire is produced by cognition; action is produced by desire;
indeed, activity is produced by action, and its result is said to be produced by that [activity]. (1)

If there exists knowledge regarding that [subject], then the meaning of the word "question" (praśna) does not cohere; furthermore, the faults of "grinding what is already ground" (piṣṭapeṣaṇa) and "proving what is already established" (siddhasādhana) arise. In the question, "What is the proof for the existence of God? the word "what" (kiṃ) itself is an auxiliary. There are six examples of the word "what": 1) "qualified by an unspecified particular," as in "Of what nature is the referent of the word 'gavaya'? 2) "To whom, O Lord, do you resort to the edge of the sky, having surrendered the Kuru clan? 3) "The sense of slightness" (īṣadartha).

As in: "He has nothing whatsoever. "Excellence" (*atiśaya*), as in: "How he acts with such boldness! and so forth; here the understanding is that he acts with exceeding boldness. "Question" (*praśna*), as in: "What is this? Is he sleeping, or is he paralyzed? and so forth; "Doubt" (*vitarka*) is the speaker’s cognition characterized by uncertainty, as in: "Is it the moon, or is it a lotus? Six meanings appear for the prefix *pra-* due to the following distinctions: 1) non-apprehension of a distinction (*anādhṛtaviśeṣa*), 2) distinguished (*viśiṣṭa*), 3) slight (*īṣadartha*), 4) excellence (*atiśaya*), 5) inquiry (*praśna*), and 6) censure (*kutsā*). However, in the *Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya*, only four meanings are specified:

"In whatever manner another person explains a particular object of one's own question through their statement, that very object should be expressed by the respondent in exactly the same way through speech; such is that meaning."

"Whatever may be the subject matter of a question, that must be expressed by speech itself; thus it becomes defined. This very point has been established by you as well through this very statement, wherein the speaker has stated the subject matter of his own inquiry. Thus [ends the argument]. Furthermore, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*).
Co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*) consists in being a generator of the cognition of a single object through the relation of identity, while possessing distinct case-endings.

"The pot is blue," "the Great Ninth," "supreme sovereignty," and "see Devadatta cooking"—regarding these, grammarians say that the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* [are used] after the present indicative (*laṭ*). Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*) consists in having a common substratum (*ekādhikaraṇavṛttikatva*), as in the definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*): "the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) which has the same substratum as the reason. Alternatively, they say that co-referentiality consists in being concomitant with both sides of a dichotomy (*koṭidvayasahacaritatva*), as for example: "fire is co-referential with smoke and the absence of smoke. It also consists in having the same mental construction (*samānākārakatva*).

Regarding one's own [cognition], "having the same form" (*samānakārakatva*) consists in possessing a qualificative-ness (*prakāritā*) delimited by being qualified by that [object] which is delimited by being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) of that very [cognition]. Furthermore, subtle observers maintain that it consists in having a state of objecthood (*viṣayatā*) characterized by a relation of the determined (*nirūpya*) and the determiner (*nirūpaka*) exactly as it exists in one's own [cognition]. Now, the question arises: what is the nature of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatva*)?

Nor should it be said that being presented by the function of a base (*prakṛti*) is what constitutes being the meaning of a base; for there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix whose meaning is an agent, object, or the like, since the function [of denoting] does not apply to that which is qualified by such a suffix. This is because, as in the case of a *kṛt*-suffix denoting an action (e.g., *rāgaḥ*, *pākaḥ*), a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) is admitted there. Nor should it be argued that there is excessive complexity (*gaurava*) due to the infinity of the sequences of *kṛt*-suffixes; for the definition has been refined to state that "being the meaning of a base" consists in being the object of the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by the base.

Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as *pacantau paṭhantau* ("the two cooking and reading"), the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) would also incur the status of being the primary meaning (*prakṛtyarthatva*), because the property of being the object prompted by the application of the entire complex ending in the suffix *śatṛ* exists even in the root-meaning; for the definition [of the primary meaning] is: "being the object of a verbal cognition prompted by a relation (*vṛtti*) with respect to that which is delimited by a property pervaded by the delimiting condition of the objectivehood (*uddeśyatā*) as determined by the prescriptivehood (*vidheyatā*) residing in the suffix."

In reality, however, the definition of being the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatva*) is: "the state of being an object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) brought about by [a word], which resides in that which possesses a property-relation (*nirūpyatā*) determined by a relatum-ship (*nirūpakatā*) co-located with the objective-ness (*uddeśyatā*) determined by the predicated-ness (*vidheyatā*) residing in the suffix. This must be sought further ahead.
And [the state of] being delimited by the delimiter of the qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*) is as follows:

The meaning is: "not being characterized by a delimitor that resides in something possessing its own absence. That is to say, it is the state of not possessing a delimitedness (*avacchedyatva*) that is itself characterized by a delimitorhood (*avacchedakatā*) residing in an entity that possesses its own absence. The resultant meaning is: the state of not possessing a delimitedness that is characterized by a characterizing relation (*nirūpakatā*) residing in a delimitorhood that resides in an entity distinct from the delimitor of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*). And [the phrase] "being delimited by its own delimitorhood" means...

The absence of the property of being a relatum (*nirūpyatva*) which is itself qualified by a delimitation (*avacchedyatā*) that is, in turn, qualified by a delimitation residing in an entity distinct from the delimitation residing in itself.

(An Analysis of the Causes of Verbal Cognition) Now, if it is asked: "If verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is simply the state of being an object of a cognition produced by words, what are its causes? [The answer is: expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), contiguity (*āsatti*), and intention (*tātparya*).

In the cognition "the pot is blue" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), there is a qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the pot, which is delimited by its own nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*), delimited by pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*), and delimited by that deliminate-ness (*avacchedyatā*) which is itself characterized by a non-delimited deliminate-ness (*niravacchinna-avacchedakatā*) residing in pot-ness; this [pot-ness] is further characterized by a mode-ness (*prakāratā*) delimited by blue-ness (*nīlatva*), which is itself delimited by a non-delimited deliminate-ness residing in blue-ness, as determined by the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*). This is the [qualificand-ness] residing in the pot.

The causal factor of expectancy is the knowledge of expectancy, which consists in the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the word "pot" ending in a *sup*-suffix with the word "blue" ending in a *sup*-suffix, as a cause for a verbal cognition characterized by having such a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*).

To prevent the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) "the pot, the objectness, the bringing, the action" from arising from the sentence "ghaṭaḥ karmatvam ānayanam kṛtiḥ," the knowledge of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)—in the form of the co-occurrence of the accusative case-ending immediately following the word "ghaṭa"—is the cause for [the cognition] delimited by the state of being the bringing which is the relatum of the objectness residing in the pot. And it should not be asked: "How can there be syntactic expectancy, given that different connections are observed in cases such as 'ayam eti putro rājñaḥ puruṣo 'pasāryatām' (this son of the king is coming; let the man be removed)? For it is stated that the intention (*tātparya*) of the word "king" is grasped together with the word "son."

The result is that *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) is the relation between each respective word and its capacity to generate the cognition of the logical connection (*anvaya*). [This is defined as follows: with respect to a verbal cognition characterized by a subjecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by the nature of "pot" (*ghaṭatva*), which is itself delimited by a nature-relation (*svarūpasambandha*) possessing a delimitedness (*avacchedyatā*) determined by an undelimited delimiting factor (*niravacchinnāvacchedakatā*) residing in the nature of "pot-ness," and which is further characterized by a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) delimited by the nature of "blue" (*nīlatva*), which is itself delimited by a nature-relation possessing a delimitedness determined by an undelimited delimiting factor residing in the nature of "blueness" (*nīlatva*)—this blueness being delimited by a relation delimited by non-difference (*abhedasambandha*). [In other words, for a verbal cognition to arise, there must be an expectancy consisting of the mutual requirement between the meanings of the words.]

The cause is the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatājñāna*) qualified by the presentation of "potness" (delimited by *ghaṭatva*) produced by the word "pot," which is itself qualified by the presentation of "blueness" (delimited by *nīlatva*) produced by the word "blue. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that such a knowledge of semantic competency is impossible prior to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), because the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is in some cases entirely unprecedented? This need not be said; for immediately after the utterance of the sentence, through the recollection of the respective word-meanings, there is the possibility of a knowledge of semantic competency in the form of either doubt or certainty.

Since a mental object (*bauddhapadārtha*) must necessarily be admitted in accordance with dreams and the like, there is no dispute regarding the comprehension of syntactic connection (*anvayabodha*) once such a mental object is accepted. "He sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*) is a counter-example; for the agency of fire as the instrument (*karaṇakatva*) in the act of sprinkling is incompatible (*ayogyatva*). In reality, however, the cognition of compatibility is not the cause of verbal comprehension; rather, because the absence of fire's status as an instrument of sprinkling is understood through worldly experience, there is no verbal comprehension in that case due to the semantic impossibility (*arthānupapatti*)—this is the profound point.

In reality, however, the sentence "he sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*) does indeed exist, because of the statement: "For even regarding an object that is absolutely non-existent, verbal expression produces cognition. It is for this very reason that words such as "son of a barren woman" possess the status of nominal bases (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, it would lead to the consequence of ridicule if one were asked, "How can you speak of sprinkling with fire, which is not liquid? Since mental objects (*bauddha-padārtha*) are necessary to account for dreams and the like, the sentence "he sprinkles with fire" is not used in common worldly discourse because its lack of empirical validity (*aprāmāṇya*) is apprehended there.

The knowledge of the speaker's intention (*tātparyajñāna*), which takes the form "the sentence 'the blue pot' generates a verbal cognition characterized by a qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by the nature of being a pot (*ghaṭatva*), which is delimited by a non-delimited delimitorhood (*niravacchinnāvacchedakatā*) residing in potness, and is related through a self-linking relation (*svarūpasambandha*) that is delimited by a modehood (*prakāratā*) delimited by blueness, which is related through a self-linking relation that is delimited by a delimitability (*avacchedyatā*) determined by a non-delimited delimitorhood residing in blueness, which is delimited by the relation of identity (*abhedasambandha*)."

Each of these is a cause for the comprehension of verbal meaning. For this very reason, in cases such as "bring the *saindhava*," when there is a cognition of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*), the understanding of salt arises at the time of a meal due to that cognition of intention, whereas the understanding of a horse arises in the context of a journey; thus, the consistency of worldly usage is maintained. Furthermore, the elders declare that the apprehension of word-power (*śakti*) occurs through grammar, comparison, lexicons, the statements of reliable persons, and usage; and they say it also occurs from the remainder of a sentence, from the function of a word, and from the proximity of a word whose meaning is already established.

It must be asked: how can the knowledge of *tātparya* (speaker’s intention) be the cause [of verbal comprehension] if, by the rule of the learned (*śiṣṭa-niyama*) and through context (*prakaraṇa*) alone, the meaning of the word *saindhava* is understood in its respective instances? For, based on the experience of what the *tātparya* is in that context and what kind of *tātparya*-qualified context it is, the context itself is determined by the *tātparya*; thus, it is accepted that the knowledge of *tātparya* alone is the cause of verbal comprehension by the most parsimonious method.

For this very reason, the formulation of the maxim—"from the intention regarding multiple meanings, there is the comprehension of the specific"—is rendered meaningful. For this very reason, in the case of a sentence uttered by a parrot or a sentence uttered by a silent person, the knowledge of the intention of the teacher or of God, who possesses that inherent nature, is universally accepted as the cause, as there is no other recourse.

A Note on the Absence of Investigation Regarding Immediate Succession: Now, it might be argued that it is untenable for expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), semantic competency (*yogyatā*), proximity (*āsatti*), and speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) to be the causes with respect to that which is delimited by being the object-cause (*prakāratva*) of a verbal cognition whose content is "a single blue pot. Furthermore, if multiple causes are admitted, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the cognitions produced by each of them individually.

If it is argued: "In a case where there is a cognition having 'pot' as its qualificandum and 'blue-ness' as its qualifier—this cognition being produced by a knowledge of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) consisting in the nature of the word 'pot' being co-uttered with the word 'blue'—there is indeed no knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), which consists in the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) of 'pot-ness' as delimited by the word 'pot' and 'blue-ness' as delimited by the word 'blue'; nevertheless, the cognition having 'pot' as its qualificandum and 'blue-ness' as its qualifier does occur. Thus, the effect exists while the cause is absent; therefore, because the cause is not subsumed under the delimitor of the causal efficacy (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), this is a logical fault (*doṣa*). Is this not so?

The knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣājñāna*)—consisting in the nature of being the word "ghaṭa" ending in the suffix *su* and occurring in immediate proximity to the word "nīla" ending in the suffix *su*—is the cause for that which is delimited by the status of a verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*) characterized by a qualificandumhood (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by the property of being a pot (*ghaṭatva*), which is itself determined by a subjecthood (*prakāratā*) delimited by the property of blueness (*nīlatva*) and related through the relation of identity (*abheda*). This [cognition] arises immediately after the knowledge of expectancy consisting in the nature of being the word "ghaṭa" ending in the suffix *su* and occurring in immediate proximity to the word "nīla" ending in the suffix *su*.

With respect to a verbal cognition characterized by the property of being a verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhitva*)—which has as its qualificandum-ness delimited by *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) and is determined by a mode-ness delimited by *nīlatva* (blueness), related through the relation of non-difference (*abheda*), and which arises immediately after the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) of a pot delimited by *ghaṭatva* produced by the word "pot" and a [quality] delimited by *nīlatva* produced by the word "blue"—the knowledge of the semantic competency (*yogyatājñāna*) consisting in the mental presentation of [the quality] delimited by *nīlatva* produced by the word "blue" and [the pot] delimited by *ghaṭatva* produced by the word "pot" is the cause.

Thus, with respect to the verbal cognition—characterized by having "pot" as its qualificand (viśeṣya) and "non-difference" (*abheda*) as its relation (*saṃsarga*), and having "blue" (*nīla*) as its qualifier (*prakāra*)—which arises immediately after the knowledge of the speaker's intention (*tātparya-jñāna*) in the form "the sentence 'the pot is blue' generates such a verbal cognition," the knowledge of the intention qualified by the meanings of the words "blue" and "pot" is the cause.

In this manner, the knowledge of non-proximity (*asattijñāna*)—in the form of the property of being the word "pot" occurring immediately after the word "blue"—is the cause for the verbal cognition that has "pot" as its qualificandum and "non-difference" as its relation, which arises immediately after the knowledge of non-proximity. By introducing "immediately following such-and-such a cause" in this way, there is an absence of the state of not being subsumed under the delimitor of effectness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for a remote cause.

The knowledge of proximity (*āsatti*) is also a cause for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Proximity consists in a word being in the position immediately following another specific word. Alternatively, proximity consists in a specific word being in the position immediately following another specific word, such that it is the object of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) by virtue of generating the cognition of the word-meanings produced by those respective words through a function conducive to the intended verbal comprehension at hand.

In such cases as "The mountain has been eaten by Agnimān Devadatta," the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the referent of the word "mountain" (*giripadārtha*) and the referent of the word "eaten" (*bhuktapadārtha*) is not the object of expectation, because there is no intended meaning (*tātparya*) for those two. Rather, it is only the connection between the referent of the word "mountain" and the referent of the word "Agnimān" that constitutes the semantic coherence (*asatti*). Thus, verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arises through the mediation of words qualified by their respective referents.

And thus: there is a property-locusness (*avacchedyatā*) which is determined by a non-restricted non-limitingness (*niravacchinnāvacchedakatā*) residing in "blueness" (*nīlatva*), that non-limitingness being delimited by the relation of identity (*abhedasambandha*); this property-locusness belongs to a modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in "blue," which is delimited by the relation of self-linking (*svarūpasambandha*) and itself delimited by "blueness"; this modehood is further determined by a non-restricted non-limitingness residing in "potness" (*ghaṭatva*); and this non-limitingness is determined by a property-locusness which possesses such a non-limitingness.

The knowledge of the *sattā* (co-occurrence) consisting in the nature of the word "ghaṭa" (pot)—which possesses the power (*śakti*) as determined by the meaning of the word "ghaṭa" occurring immediately after the word "nīla," and which is qualified by the presentation [of the object] dependent on the knowledge of the *vṛtti* residing in the word "nīla"—is the cause for a verbal cognition characterized by the state of being a verbal cognition possessing such a qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*). This qualificandumness resides in the pot, is delimited by the property of "pot-ness," and is delimited by the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*). The example and counter-example are quite clear.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of silent poetry (*mauniśloka*) and the like, there is no cognition of proximity (*āsatti*), because the status of being an utterance—which arises from the impact of the throat, palate, and other articulatory organs—is absent, and consequently, the status of being a single word consisting of a collection of phonemes is lacking. This is not a fault, because even in the absence of an actual word, the inferential knowledge of a word is necessarily required; otherwise, in the absence of the cause that is the knowledge of a word, verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) itself would be impossible in cases such as silent poetry.

Likewise, the essential point is that when the intention (*tātparya*) of the sage is understood to consist in generating the comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) between two words, inferential knowledge (*anumānika-jñāna*) indeed arises between those two words without any intervention.

One might ask: "In cases such as 'He cooks rice in a pot' (*sthālyām odanaṃ pacati*) or 'Devadatta goes home' (*devadatto gṛhaṃ gacchati*), since there is an intervention by words like *odana* (rice), how can the cognition of proximity (*āsatti*)—which is a cause [of verbal comprehension]—be present there? This should not be said, because proximity is not absent, given that [the words] possess a suitability for the intended connection (*prakṛtānvayabodhānukūlatva*) and are the objects of a specific intention (*tātparya*). Intention (*tātparya*) is the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) in the form: "I utter this word or sentence in order to convey this meaning.
Furthermore, [proximity is defined as] being unconditioned by that which does not delimit itself.

It is precisely the state of not being qualified by any other delimitor (*avacchedaka*) distinct from the delimitor of its own specifier (*nirūpaka*). And this "distinctness" is [to be understood] either through the relation of co-existence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or through relations such as deviation (*vyabhicāritva*). Consequently, even if a non-delimiter of itself is unestablished in cases such as "this has the property of being knowable" (*prameyatvam idam asti*), there is no fault.
Furthermore, it is the state of not being delimited by that which is a non-delimiter of itself.

Even though there exists a mutual relationship of the determined (*nirūpya*) and the determiner (*nirūpaka*), [the definition of the property] consists in being different from that which possesses a delimitorship (*avacchedakatā*) other than the delimitorship qualified by its own [corresponding] delimitedness. Here, "possessing delimitorship" is by way of the relation of being delimited by the subjecthood (*viśeṣyatva*) as determined by the modehood (*prakāratā*) which is itself delimited by it. And this "being delimited" is common to both direct and indirect [delimitation]. Indirectly, it is by way of the relation of being delimited by the subjecthood as determined by the modehood which is itself delimited by that [delimitor].

The property of being delimited by the qualificandness (viśeṣyatva) as determined by the mode (prakāratā) delimited by the delimitor of the ultimate limit (niṣṭhāvacchedakatva) residing in "manhood" (puruṣatva) does not exist, even indirectly, in the delimitingness (avacchedakatā) residing in "selfhood" (svatva),
nor in the sequential order (ānupūrvī).

The sequential order (*pūrvāparībhāva*) of phonemes is as follows: in the word *ghaṭa* and similar examples, there is the letter *gha*, followed by the letter *a*, followed by the letter *ṭa*, followed by the letter *a*. The term *anupūrvam* means "suitable for what precedes"; *anupūrvī* is simply that same sequence with a suffix added. By the rule *prajñādibhyo ’ṇ* (Pāṇini 5.4.38), the suffix *aṇ* is applied because the word belongs to the *prajñādi* group; since it ends in *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. In the case of *ghaṭa* and similar words, it consists in having the same sequential order as the word *ghaṭa*, whose denotative power (*śakti*) is delimited by individual entities possessing a neck shaped like a conch (*kambugrīvādimat*). [The compound] *gha-ṭa* is a collective (*samāhāra*) of *gha* and *ṭa*. "Having the same sequential order as that" refers to the state of being identical in its sequence to that [word].

The general definition is: "the state of having the same sequential order as that [word], while possessing those respective phonemes following each respective preceding phoneme. It should not be argued that, if this were the definition, then because the property of "having a *ṭa* following an *ā* which follows a *gha*" exists even in the word *nīlaghaṭa*, it would undesirably follow that the specific word *nīlaghaṭa* also possesses the same sequential order as the word *ghaṭa*. This is because "having the same sequential order as that word" means being a word qualified by that word.

And the property of being distinctive (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [of one word with respect to another] is by means of both relations: (1) not being composed of that which is delimited by a delimitor of its own constituenthood (*svaghaṭakatānavacchedaka*), and (2) having its occurrence (*vṛttitva*) in itself as delimited by a relation that is delimited by a non-delimiter of its own constituenthood (*svaghaṭakatānavacchedaka*). Thus, the state of having the same sequential order (*samānānupūrvīkatva*) as the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) does not, in the case of the word "blue-pot" (*nīlaghaṭa*), consist merely in being composed of that which is delimited by blueness (*nīlatva*)—which is a non-delimiter of the constituenthood of the word "pot"—and therefore there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) from the definition.

Nor should it be argued that, although "wordhood" (*padatva*) is a recurring property by virtue of its relation to Pāṇini’s convention—just as "being subsequent" (*paratva*) is a recurring property—it would follow that words such as *saraḥ*, *rasaḥ*, *nadī*, *dīnaḥ*, *rājan*, *jarā*, *tālaḥ*, and *latā* would possess identical sequential order (*samānupūrvīkatva*). This is not a fault, because when the third relation—"the state of possessing a property that delimits the causality for the cognition of one's own meaning"—is introduced, the causal properties differ due to the difference between the meanings of words such as *latā* and *tāla*. Thus, there is no error.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that when the third relation is posited, one must state a *vārttika* rule that "an indeclinable (*nipāta*) devoid of meaning should be designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)," because in examples such as *vai*, *tu*, *hi*, and *iti*—which serve solely for the purpose of filling out the meter—there would be no identity of sequence (*samānānupūrvīkatva*) with those [meaningful] items due to the absence of any communicative content. For the identity of sequence with a particular item resides in that very item itself; for instance, the identity of sequence with the word *ghaṭa* resides only in the word *ghaṭa*, and not in the phrase *nīlaghaṭa*.

The property that serves as the delimitor of the pervasion (*paryāpti*) of the objectivity (*viṣayatā*) residing in the cognition—which is co-extensive with the objectivity delimited by the nature of being a locus of difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the objectivity delimited by the nature of *a* (the letter 'a'), which in turn is delimited by the objectivity delimited by the nature of *t* (the letter 't'), which is itself delimited by the objectivity delimited by the nature of *tt* (the sequence 'tt'), which is further delimited by the objectivity delimited by the nature of *a* (the letter 'a'), and which is delimited by the objectivity delimited by its own locus—is the property of having the same phonetic sequence (*samānānupūrvīkatva*) as "pot" (*ghaṭa*) in the case of a pot. Similarly, the property of having the same phonetic sequence as "cloth" (*paṭa*) and so forth is to be understood in the case of cloth and so forth; this is the undisputed method.
This concludes the investigation into the relation (*sambandhavicāra*).

Is it not the case that everywhere the relation between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), the relation between counter-correlate and correlate (*pratiyogyanuyogibhāva*), the relation between produced and producer (*janyajanakabhāva*), and the relation between the defined and the definer (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*) are heard of in verbal cognition? In this regard, there arises this doubt: since a relation is defined by both of its constituent terms, the status of being a "relation" must belong to the qualified relation between locus and located, just as we observe that well-known relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) reside in both of their terms.

Now, it might be argued that there is no instance anywhere where two related entities—a qualified substratum and a superstratum—exist conjoined in one place; therefore, the relation between two correlates must consist solely in a single underlying connection. However, there is no fault in accepting "superstratum-ness" (*ādheyatva*) as the relation itself, provided it is proximate to the substratum by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*) in the case of the superstratum, and by way of being the determiner (*nirūpakatā*) in the case of the substratum. This is because we accept that only a property residing in the correlate (the *anuyogin*) constitutes a relation; thus, in some cases, the relation is simply "substratum-ness" (*ādhāratā*).

For example, there is the relation of being contained (*ādheyatā*) of a jar with respect to the ground, and conversely, that of the ground with respect to the jar. In expressions such as "the jar is blue," there is the property of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) in the blue and the property of being the substratum (*anuyogitā*) in the jar; in "knowledge of the jar," there is the state of being the object (*viṣayatva*) in the jar and the state of being the subject (*viṣayitva*) in the knowledge.

And thus, the moderns claim that the acceptance of "relationality" (*sambandhatva*) resides in one [entity] alone due to parsimony (*lāghava*); but is that not so? For relationality belongs to those very entities—such as the locus-hood (*ādhāratā*), the counter-correlativity of the locatedness (*ādheyatva*) determined by that locus-hood, and the correlate-hood (*anuyogitva*) determined by that counter-correlativity—which are themselves related through a mutual relationship of determiner and determined (*nirūpya-nirūpaka-bhāva*), and which are conventionally designated as the "relation between locus and located"; it does not belong to each of these individually.

In cases such as "the mountain possesses fire" (*vahnimān parvata*), if the relation is the state of being the counter-correlativity delimited by the property of fire-ness (*vahnitvāvacchinnapratiyogitva*), then just as these [delimited counter-correlativities] constitute the relation, there is no obstacle whatsoever to other properties—such as the relation between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*)—constituting the relation. Therefore, the view of the Neo-logicians (*navīna*) that "only a property residing in the locus (*anuyogin*) constitutes the relation" is not particularly superior.

In this regard, even the definition of the Grammarians (*śābdika*) is supportive: "A relation is indeed distinct from its two relata, resides in both (*dviṣṭa*), and is the regulator of the cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*)."

Regarding the expression "Caitra’s teacher’s family" (*caitrasya gurukulam*): the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) therein is that the teacher (*guru*) possesses a delimitedness (*avacchedyatā*) which is itself delimited by a delimitorhood (*avacchedakatā*) residing in teacherhood (*gurutva*), which is in turn determined by Caitra. In this context, the referent of the word "teacher" (*gurupadārtha*) is characterized by teacherhood. And teacherhood, in turn, requires determination by Caitra. Thus, because there is no further purpose [served], the word "family" (*kulam*) need not be supplied in the sentence. Now, [we consider] the knowledge of the relationship that facilitates refinement (*pariṣkāra*).

When there is a distinction in cognition, there is a corresponding distinction in the object; as is the case with the cause, so too are its relations with the objects causes. For all-pervading categories such as time and space, there exists some general relation with all other categories. For certain objects of cognition, such as jars and the like, there are four types of relations established within time: (1) temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*), (2) temporal qualifier-relation (*kālika-viśeṣaṇatā-sambandha*), and (3) the relation of being conjoined with time which is itself conjoined [with the locus]. (4) [The fourth is] the relation of being conjoined with time which is itself conjoined with [the locus].

The relation is that of being located in time which is its own substratum. Having placed its [the object's] cognition in the middle, there are the following relations: (1) the relation of being the object of a cognition whose object is itself; (2) the relation of being the object of a cognition whose subject is itself; (3) the relation of being the locus of an objecthood as determined by a cognition that determines an objecthood residing in itself; (4) the relation of being the locus of an objecthood as determined by an objecthood that is co-locus with an objecthood residing in a cognition that determines an objecthood residing in itself.

In this way, other types of relations involving qualifiers (*viśeṣa*) should also be understood. For example, just as first there is the production of a stone and subsequently a house is built with that stone, so too, having first acquired a cognition of the jar and the "jar-ness" as distinct entities, one subsequently attains determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) upon the cognition of their inherence (*samavāya*). However, the initial cognition takes the form of "the jar and jar-ness," which is indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*). It is precisely through the cognition of the relation that determinate cognition is established. Among all relations and qualifiers, there exists a mutual relationship of the defined (*nirūpya*) and the definer (*nirūpaka*).

Just as when a person standing on the ground has a relationship of being supported (*ādheyatva*) with the ground, there must necessarily be a relationship of being the support (*ādhāratva*) for the person by the ground; and if a tree’s branch has a relationship of being a constituent part (*avayavatva*) with the entity that is the tree, then the branch also has a relationship of being the whole (*avayavitva*) with the tree.

The unique relations that determine universals—which include conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and the relation called essential nature (*svarūpa*)—are counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) and sub-correlativity (*anuyogitā*). For example, in the expression "the face is like the moon," the meaning is that the face is the sub-correlative of a similarity whose counter-correlative is the moon; here, the relation that determines and ascertains the relation of similarity is indeed counter-correlativity with respect to the moon, while the relation of sub-correlativity resides in the face.

The result is that counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), while substratumness (*anuyogitva*) takes the form of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). For example, in the case of "the absence of a jar on the ground," the absence has counter-positiveness with respect to the jar and substratumness with respect to the ground. That which possesses objecthood (*viṣayatva*) or objectness (*viṣayatā*) is the particular (*viśeṣa*). That which possesses subjecthood (*viṣayitā*) is the subject (*viṣayin*). That which possesses qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) is the category of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). And that which possesses modehood (*prakāratā*) is the mode (*prakāra*).

That which possesses the relation of being produced (*janyatā-sambandha*) is itself the produced; that which possesses the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) is the substratum; and that which possesses ownership (*svāmitva*) is the owner. Wherever a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭa-jñāna*) arises, it occurs there only through the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) among multiple entities.

In the philosophical treatises, there is the usage of the terms *samaṣṭi* (the collective) and *vyaṣṭi* (the individual). In a forest consisting of a thousand or a hundred thousand trees, the singular form "forest" (*vanam*) is employed with the intention of referring to the collective whole; in that very same collective form, the use of the term *samaṣṭi* is appropriate. If, in that same forest, one employs the word "trees" (*vṛkṣāḥ*) with the intention of referring to the number belonging to the parts, then the use of the term *vyaṣṭi* is appropriate. In the context of worldly usage, the cognition of each individual object such as a pot or a cloth constitutes the form of the *vyaṣṭi*.

The knowledge of God (*īśvarajñāna*) is of the nature of a collective whole (*samaṣṭi*). What is the knowledge of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*)? When a person has previously had the cognition "this is blue clothing," that same person subsequently acquires a cognition in the form "I know the blue clothing. This second cognition takes the first cognition as its object. In this context, the second cognition alone is of the nature of *anuvyavasāya*. The non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition regarding God is not of the nature of *anuvyavasāya*, because a second cognition [of that first cognition] does not exist [in the case of God].
The essential meaning is that the state of being *anuvyavasāya* consists in being a cognition produced by another cognition.

In accordance with the sūtra of Gautama, "The individual, the form, and the universal are the meaning of a word," the denotative power (śakti) resides in the pot, the pot-ness, and their inherence; thus, in the cognition of a pot, pot-ness appears as related to the pot by way of inherence (samavāya).

Now, what is the meaning of the statement "pot-ness (ghaṭatva) appears in the pot by way of inherence" (samavāya)? Taking the state of being defined (nirūpitatva) as the meaning of the locative case, does this mean that "pot-ness has a subsistence (vṛttitva) delimited by the relation of inherence as defined by the pot," or does it mean that "the pot has a substratum-hood (adhikaraṇatva) defined by pot-ness as delimited by the relation of inherence"? In both cases, when the relation of identity (abheda-sambandha) is applied to subsistence and substratum-hood, the result is that the pot and pot-ness are understood in this manner.
If difference (*bheda*) and relation (*sambandha*) were accepted [as distinct categories], the intended cognition would not arise; let those rich in wisdom consider what the answer is to this doubt.

Now, in cases such as "the ground possesses a jar" (*ghaṭavad bhūtalam*), there is a universally recognized cognition characterized by a qualificandumness delimited by "ground-ness" (*bhūtalatva*) as determined by a qualifierhood delimited by "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and restricted by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). This is the process of analysis therein: the result is that the jar is apprehended in the ground by way of conjunction.

What is the meaning of the statement that "a jar is located on the ground by way of conjunction" (*saṃyogena*)? Does it mean that the jar has the property of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) with respect to conjunction, or rather that it possesses the property of occurrence (*vṛttitva*) as delimited by the relation of conjunction as defined by the ground? Furthermore, what kind of relation exists between such a locus-ness and occurrence on the one hand, and the ground and the jar on the other? If the relation between those two [properties] and those two [substances] were one of non-difference (*abheda*), then the established difference between them would be contradicted.

When there arises a desire to know the specific relation between the state of being an occurrence (*vṛttitva*) and the state of being a substratum (*adhikaraṇatva*), if one introduces the qualification of being delimited by a specific relation, then upon further inquiry as to whether those two [relations] are distinct or non-distinct, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) results. If it is argued that one accepts the meaning of the sentence by eventually reaching a point where no further relation is admitted, then it would be more logical to simply not admit any relation at the very outset; why resort to the maxim of "covering the head while touching the nose"? Therefore, one must seek a further answer: that there is indeed some purely mental cognition devoid of relations.
This also applies to the *tatpuruṣa* compound.

A *tatpuruṣa* compound is that which, through its own formal connection, serves to bring about the cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) of a specific meaning with another meaning that qualifies it. For example, *grāmagata* ("gone to the village") and the like.

Furthermore, according to others, a *tatpuruṣa* is a compound whose first member has its case-ending elided (such as the second case), provided that the name of the subsequent member is not devoid of the technical definition (*lakṣaṇā*) induced by compounding. For example, *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man") and the like.
And there is also the *karmadhāraya*.

Regarding the specific types of compounds, the rule is: "A *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members have a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is a *karmadhāraya*. Here, this should be considered: in a *karmadhāraya*, there is neither a primary denotative power (*śakti*) nor a secondary indicative power (*lakṣaṇā*) for the qualified meaning, since the intended cognition of the relationship is established even without those two. Grammarians (*śābdika*), however, postulate a distinct power for the qualified meaning in every compound.

Let there be a definition: a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of two names that are successive and immediate, where the meaning of one name is capable of being construed with the meaning of the other name as being identical (*tādātmya*) within a single substratum (*dharmin*). For example, in expressions such as *nīlotpalam* ("blue lotus"), the meaning of the word "blue" is construed as identical with the meaning of the word "lotus. Similarly, in cases such as *puruṣasiṃha* ("man-lion"), the meaning indicated by the latter member—namely, something similar to a lion—is construed as identical with the meaning of the word "man."

The term "near the jar" (*kumbhasya samīpam*) conveys the understanding of proximity; since a word such as *upa-kumbha* does not convey a relation of identity (*tādātmya*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case.

Others, however, define a *karmadhāraya* as a compound consisting of two names having the same referent (*tulyārtha*) and being devoid of any indication (*lakṣaṇā*) necessitated by the compound itself—such as in the case of *nīlotpala* ("blue lotus"). Here, because the expression *pañcamūlī* ("five roots") also possesses the property of having two names with the same referent, the qualifier "devoid of indication necessitated by the compound" is added to exclude it. Furthermore, the qualifier "having the same referent" is added to exclude *dvandva* compounds, such as *dhava-khadira*.

In the case of *nīlotpalam* ("blue lotus"), although there is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) in the word *nīla* for the locus of the quality "blue," there is no lack of pervasion [in the definition] because that [indication] is not necessitated by a compound. Furthermore, it should be understood that the application of the definition is possible because the two names have the same referent. In examples such as *stokapaktā* ("one who cooks slightly"), there is indeed a *karmadhāraya* compound with adverbial qualifiers (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).

In expressions such as *mahākaviḥ* (great poet) and *mahāvijñaḥ* (greatly wise), since the meaning of another name (*mahā-*) is understood as being non-different from a single part of the meaning of the base noun (*kavi-* or *vijña-*), just as it is in the case of [the suffix] *-tva* in *kavitva*, the status of a *karmadhāraya* compound is possible. However, in cases such as *stokapaktā* (one who cooks slightly), if the accusative suffix (*am*) denotes identity (*tādātmya*), a *tatpuruṣa* compound is indeed possible. It is not correct to claim that a compound with adverbial qualifiers (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) is ungrammatical, for compounds such as *stokanamrā stanābhyām* (slightly bent by the breasts) have been employed by Kālidāsa and others.

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, there is neither direct denotation (*śakti*) nor indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Since the meaning of the word "blue" can be construed with the meaning of the word "lotus" through the very relation of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*), one need not admit either direct denotation or indication. For this very reason, the *karmadhāraya* is simpler than the *tatpuruṣa*. To illustrate: in the Vedic injunction "One should cause the *niṣādasthapati* to sacrifice," the *karmadhāraya* is simpler—due to the absence of indication and other such factors—when compared to the *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds.

In this regard, the following must be considered: although the Niṣāda—a specific mixed caste included among the Śūdras—is excluded from the study of the Veda in general by the prohibition, "Women and Śūdras shall not study," nevertheless, the study of the Niṣāda is postulated as being sufficient for the sacrifice alone; this is because the specific scriptural injunction, "One should cause the Niṣāda-sthapati to perform a sacrifice," would otherwise be inexplicable.

And thus, in the general rule "women and Śūdras [are excluded from study]," it must be stated that the term *adhyayana* (study) refers specifically to study other than that which is [otherwise] obtained [by right]. By this, the prohibition of study—other than that required for the performance of sacrifice—is established for the Niṣāda, whereas for other Śūdras, a total prohibition of all study is established. This is the *kāraka*.

A *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is that which, as a meaning manifested by a particular verbal root (*dhātu*), appears as a mode of the universal (*anvaya-prakāra*) within the meaning manifested by that same verbal root; that is, it is a *kāraka* with respect to the action of such a kind manifested by that verbal root. For example: in "falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt patati*) and "fears the tiger" (*vyāghrād bibheti*); in "gives to the Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇāya dadāti*) and "is angry with the son" (*putrāya krudhyati*); in "cuts with the axe" (*dātreṇa chinatti*) and "knows as a jar-ness" (*ghaṭatvena jānāti*); in "cooks in the pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*) and "appears in the mother-of-pearl" (*śuktau bhāsate*); in "goes to the village" (*grāme gacchati*) and "sees the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ paśyati*); and in "is cooked by Caitra" (*caitreṇa pacyate*) and "by the jar" (*ghaṭena*).

In expressions such as *bhūyate* ("is fallen"), the disjunction (*vibhāga*) and so forth, which are presented by the fifth case (*pañcamī*) and other cases, appear as qualifiers (*prakārībhūya*) within the meaning of the verbal root—such as "falling" (*patana*) and the like—which is itself the meaning of roots like *pat*. Thus, in the context of the specific action presented by each respective verbal root, disjunction and so forth function as the *kāraka*.

Others, however, maintain that when a case-meaning (*sub-artha*), as delimited by a certain nominal meaning (*nāmārtha*), is construed with a certain meaning of a verbal root, that [nominal meaning] is designated as a *kāraka* in relation to that meaning of the verbal root. Consequently, in examples such as *vṛkṣāt patati* ("he falls from the tree"), even the tree and so forth receive the designation of a *kāraka*, such as the ablative (*apādāna*), in relation to the action of falling.

Others, however, the grammarians (*śābdika*), maintain that a *kāraka* is an object that has become a qualifier of the action (*kriyā*). Some, moreover, define the state of being a *kāraka* as "being connected with the meaning of a case-ending that is itself connected with the action. This definition applies correctly because in the case of the object (*karman*) and other *kārakas*, there is indeed a connection with the meaning of a nominal suffix (*sub-vibhakti*) that is connected with the action. In sentences such as "Caitra cooks the rice" (*caitrasya taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), however, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because the relation expressed by the genitive suffix in "Caitra's" (*caitrasya*)—which relates to Caitra as a possessor—is connected with the referent of the noun "rice" (*taṇḍula*), and not with the action. Even in cases like "Caitra's cooking" (*caitrasya pacati*), the understanding occurs only through the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of a word such as "rice."

Because the relation denoted by the genitive case is satisfied by its connection with the meaning of a noun alone, and because an action is satisfied by its connection with [factors] such as the object (*karman*) alone, there is a lack of mutual expectancy between them. In examples such as *odanasya paktā* ("the cooker of rice") and *maitrasya pākaḥ* ("Maitra's cooking"), the genitive expressing the sense of the object or the agent is indeed a "case-ending of a factor" (*kāraka-vibhakti*), since it is prescribed by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*. For this very reason, a relation does not possess the status of a "factor," as it lacks connection with an action. Others, however, maintain that a "factor" is a meaning that constitutes a mode of the action, and that it is of six kinds.

Grammarians maintain that the *śeṣa* (residual) relation is intended as a connection distinct from the distinctions of agent (*kartṛ*), object (*karman*), and so forth. For this very reason, in such instances as "A physician should treat with his own medicines those who are gurus, Brahmins, ascetics, and the destitute," and "That is Lakṣmī who benefits others," the understanding arises precisely through the mental supply (*adhyāhāra*) of the nouns "in illness" and "in calamity" respectively. The underlying point is this: here, the relation denoted by the genitive case connects only with the meaning of the supplied noun, and not with the verb; therefore, this is not a genitive of the *kāraka* (case-role).

Regarding this, Gadādharabhaṭṭācārya states that the word "roga" (disease) need not be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). He maintains that even though the genitive sense of relation (*sambandha*) connects with the meaning of the verbal root, this is not a case of a "kāraka-vibhakti" (a case ending denoting a grammatical participant), but rather an *upapada-vibhakti* (a case ending used for a word forming part of a compound). If, without supplying an ellipsis, the connection of the genitive sense with the action is considered authoritative, then "kārakatva" (the state of being a kāraka) should be understood as the property of being connected with any one of the six [grammatical relations], such as agency (*kartṛtva*), objecthood (*karmatva*), and so forth, which are connected to the action.

For this very reason, in expressions such as "one kills the leopard for its skin," even the cause (*nimitta*) and so forth do not possess the status of a *kāraka*. Grammarians (*śābdika*), however, state that the status of a *kāraka* consists in being the object of a cognition regarding the fitness to be a generator of action.
Now follows the determination of *saṅgati* (logical connection):
It is *prasaṅga* (occasion), *upodghāta* (introduction), *hetutā* (causality), and likewise *avasara* (opportunity).
When there is unity of purpose and unity of action, a sixfold association is recognized.

Prasaṅgatva (the state of being a relevant consequence) is the quality of that which has been remembered being unfit for neglect. In this context, "of that which has been remembered" means of that which has been recalled through its connection with a previously mentioned subject. "Unfit for neglect" means having a nature that is the opposite of being an object of aversion or indifference; in other words, it is a nature delimited by being an object of inquiry (*jijñāsā*). The mention of "that which has been remembered" is intended to establish that such recollection serves as the motive for stating the immediate sequence of the inquiry. Furthermore, to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to cases such as incidental introductions (*upodghāta*), the phrase "being distinct from the five types beginning with incidental introduction" must also be included in the definition.

And thus, the refined definition [of *saṅgati*] is: being a non-delimitant of the state of being an object of aversion, while being distinct from the five types beginning with *upoddhāta*, and while being an object of recollection through a connection with a previously mentioned subject matter. The meaning is: that which is defined immediately after the definition of another possesses a *saṅgati* (connection) determined by that [other].
And the nature of *upoddhāta* is as follows:

The state of being an *upapādaka* (a supporting factor) for the subject at hand (*prakṛta*). This very point has been stated in such passages as: "The wise know *upodghāta* to be a reflection intended for the establishment of the subject. In this context, being an *upapādaka* means being a generator of a resolution (*nirvāha*). And that is experienced in two ways: in some cases as a means of establishing a constituent part of the subject, and in other cases otherwise.

Furthermore, the unity of the resolver (*nirvāhakaikya*) consists in being resolvable by a single resolver; that is to say, while being distinct from that [subject], being resolvable by the resolver of that [subject].

The identity of effect (*kāryyaikya*) consists in being the motivator of a single effect. The essential definition is: being that which is brought about by that which brings it about, while being distinct from it. However, in some instances, the reading "in the state of having a single effect through being a bringer-about" (*nirvāhakaikakāryattve*) is found in the root verse; in that case, "being a bringer-about" (*nirvāhakatva*) should be understood as being a motivator (*prayojakatva*), and "having a single effect" (*ekakāryattva*) as being the effect of a single cause. Some, however, define the coherence of the identity of effect as being conducive to a single effect.

Just as the unity of the effect characterized by inference in the case of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) constitutes their *saṅgati* (relevance), this is also called "unity of purpose" (*ekakāryyatva*) and "unity of sentence" (*ekavākyatva*).

[A sentence] is that which, while being expectant (*sākāṅkṣatva*), has as its purpose the comprehension of a single meaning. Thus indeed is the Sūtra of Jaimini: "A sentence is one because of the unity of its meaning, provided that there would be expectancy if it were divided. The qualifying portion "while being expectant" is included in order to exclude the status of being a single sentence for two sentences that convey the same meaning, such as "the pot exists" (*ghaṭo 'sti*) and "the jar exists" (*kalaśo 'sti*). Expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), moreover, consists in possessing either the quality of removing an expectancy raised by [another word], or the quality of presenting an expectancy to be removed by [that other word].

When it is stated, "The ground is like a pot," if one asks, "What is a pot? and an answer is given, "That which possesses a conch-like neck and so forth," the inclusion of the requirement of "unity of meaning" (*arthaikya*) is for the purpose of precluding that these two constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*). Although such sentences do possess unity of meaning by taking some general sense into account, nevertheless, the intended meaning of the two components must be understood as the capacity to convey a single qualified object through mutual cooperation; this is what constitutes "pot-hood."

The meaning is: the state of possessing a subjectivity that pervades the subjectivity of that [absence]. That is to say, it is the state of possessing a subjectivity qualified by a subjectivity through both of these relations: being different from itself and being its pervader. For example, since the subjectivity of fire exists as a pervader of the subjectivity belonging to the cognition of the absence of fire, fire possesses the status of being a constituent of the absence of fire.

Some, however, call this by the name "delimitingness" (*avacchedakatva*). For instance, in such cases as: "the locus-ness of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvādhikaraṇatva*) must be intended with respect to the relation that constitutes the contradiction to the apprehension of the presence of the probandum; and the counter-positive-ness of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvapratiyogitva*) must be intended with respect to the relation that constitutes the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatā*)," and so forth—this is what is meant by "constituent-ness" (*ghaṭakatva*). The technical experts, however, designate it by the name "conjoining-ness" (*yojakatva*). And its synonyms are:
"runner" (*dhāvaka*), "bringer-about" (*bhāvaka*), "conjoiner" (*yojaka*), and likewise "part" (*aṃśaka*).
"The defamer and the flatterer—these six are remembered as the 'composers' (ghaṭaka).
Thus is the nature of being a composer (*ghaṭitatva*).

It consists in possessing a subject-matter that is pervaded by the subject-matter [of another]. For example, since the subject-matter of the absence of fire is pervaded by the subject-matter of fire, the absence of fire possesses the state of being composed of fire (*vahnighaṭitatva*). Or, as in cases such as "not being composed of another qualified entity," "not being composed of two qualified entities," or "being composed of the lack of coreferentiality with the counter-positive," there is the state of being composed (*ghaṭitatva*).

The nature of the "wheel" (*cakra*) consists in the occurrence of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*) based on the fact that [an entity] is dependent upon that which depends upon that which it itself depends upon. This is threefold, because it brings about [the fault] by way of origination, subsistence, and cognition. Even in cases such as the four or five sense-bases (*āyatana*), there is no excess, since each possesses the state of being dependent upon that which depends upon that which it itself depends upon.
