In the cognition "he remembers on the day," there is also the sense of identity (*abheda*) as the meaning of the locative, based on the understanding: "this person possesses devotion directed toward the Blessed One, which is pervasive throughout the duration of the day."

In the case of "the tree-top is conjoined with a monkey," the meaning of the locative case is also "delimitedness" (avacchedyatva), as evidenced by the cognition: "that which possesses a monkey-conjunction delimited by the top."

In the expression "a word in a sentence" (*vākye padam*) and "a word in a sūtra" (*sūtre padam*), the meaning of the locative case is "being a constituent part," based on the cognition that "the word is a constituent of the sentence. In the expression "the subject matter in the Veda" (*vede viṣayaḥ*), the meaning of the locative case is "being what is propounded," based on the understanding that "the subject matter is what is propounded by the Veda. In the expression "one who is doubting fire on the mountain" (*parvato vahnau saṃdihānaḥ*), the meaning of the locative case is also "being the qualificandum (or the locus)," based on the cognition that "this person possesses a doubt whose qualificandum is the mountain and whose qualifier is fire."

In the definition "a quality (guṇa) is that which possesses generality (sāmānya) while being distinct from substance (dravya) and action (karman)," the meaning of the locative case is the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) in the form of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because the verbal cognition derived from it is: "a quality is that which possesses generality as qualified by its being distinct from substance and action. In the sentence "Alas, fools desire to give away their wealth when their wealth is lost," the meaning of the locative case is also simultaneous occurrence (*samānakālikatva*), because the verbal cognition derived from it is: "fools are those who possess the desire to give at the same time as the loss of wealth."

In the expression "the son went when the father was going" (*pitari gamiṣyati gataḥ*), there arises the understanding that the agent of the act of going is one who goes at a time prior to the father's going; thus, the meaning of the locative case is *priority in time*. In the expression "the son went after the father had gone" (*pitari gate gataḥ*), there arises the understanding that the son is the agent of an act of going occurring at a time subsequent to the father's going; thus, the meaning of the locative case is *subsequent in time*. In the expression "the conjunction of the cloth with the ground" (*bhūtale paṭasaṃyogaḥ*), since we observe the verbal cognition that the conjunction has the ground as its *anuyogin* (substratum) and the cloth as its *pratiyogin* (counter-correlate), the meaning of the locative case is *anuyogitva* (the state of being the substratum).

In the expression "the contact with the ground is in the cloth," since there is a cognition of the cloth as the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) having the ground as its relatum (anuyogin), counter-correlativity (pratiyogitva) is also the meaning of the locative case.

In expressions such as "he kills the leopard for its skin" (*carmaṇi dvīpinaṃ hanti*), there arises the cognition that the agent is one who performs the killing of the leopard under the influence of a desire directed toward the skin; therefore, "being dependent on a desire whose object is itself" is also a meaning of the locative case. In the expression "the Kṣatriya is the hero among men" (*nareṣu kṣatriyaḥ śūraḥ*), there arises the cognition that the Kṣatriya is a hero who is excluded from those men who lack the quality of being a Kṣatriya—just as in the case of "the Kṣatriya is the hero of men"; therefore, "being excluded from the referent of the word ending in the locative case, which lacks the universal (jāti) that delimits the referent of the word co-occurring with itself" is also a meaning of the locative case.

In the statement "Hunger is pacified by the eating of rice," the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—namely, "this person possesses the pacification of hunger produced by the eating of rice"—is also the meaning of the locative case. In this same manner, other meanings of the locative case should also be inferred according to their true nature.

Verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is of two kinds: first, partial verbal comprehension (*khaṇḍaśābdabodha*), and subsequently, non-partial verbal comprehension (*akhaṇḍaśābdabodha*). To illustrate: in the sentence "Bring the cloth" (*paṭam ānaya*), the word "cloth" (*paṭa*) has the cloth as its meaning; the accusative case-ending has the objecthood (*karmatva*) as its meaning; the root *nī* preceded by the prefix *ā-* has "bringing" (*ānayana*) as its meaning; and according to different philosophical views, the meaning of the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*) is either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the action (*kṛti*). It is in this manner that partial verbal comprehension is considered secondary (*gauṇa*).

And being secondary (*gauṇatva*) consists in the absence of being an object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) that is produced by a mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the knowledge of [secondary] power (*śakti*). The specific verbal cognition "the locus of an activity conducive to bringing [something], which has as its qualifier the state of being the object residing in a cloth" is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*); the first [type of cognition] is for the sake of the instruction of beginners, while the second is universal. Furthermore, verbal cognition is of two kinds: Vedic and worldly (*laukika*). That which is propounded by the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and so forth is Vedic; the worldly, moreover, arises solely from the speech of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

The sequence of the process therein is as follows: in the case of "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), first there is the cognition of the word *ghaṭa*; subsequently, there is the cognition of the power residing in the word *ghaṭa*; from these two, there is the mental representation (*upasthiti*); and finally, there is the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

In such cases of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), first there is the cognition of the word, followed by the cognition of its power (*śakti*). From these two, the presentation of the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) occurs. Subsequently, due to the incompatibility of the syntactic connection and the intended meaning, there arises the cognition of the intention regarding the indicated meaning (*lakṣyapadārtha*). After that, there is the presentation of the indicated meaning, and finally, the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) having the indicated meaning as its object. Furthermore, some accept the function of suggestion (*vyañjanāvṛtti*) even in the case of the phrase "The mountains standing afar are beautiful," where [it applies] to the word *bhūdhara*.

The power of Parvata and Nṛpati is indeed equal. In the verse, "Go, O beloved, if you go, my birth shall be there indeed," she is one whose activity is death immediately following her husband's departure. However, the logicians (tārkikas) maintain that since the meaning is established through the power of denotation (śakti) alone by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa), there is no need for the power of suggestion (vyañjanā).

Following the rule that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the manifestation of properties (*dharma*)—other than universals (*jāti*) and partless adjuncts (*akhaṇḍopādhi*)—as being manifested in their own right, it is established as a rule that universals, partless adjuncts, and properties such as pots and cloths that are distinct from them, manifest only by way of some [further] property (*kiñciddharmapuraskāreṇa*).

For example, in the case of "the mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*), because there is no mention of the universal (*jāti*), the mountain-ness and the fire-ness appear solely in their own essential form (*svarūpa*) as fire-ness, and not in the form of "possessing fire-ness" (*vahnitvatva*). However, where there is linguistic usage involving the explicit mention of the qualified [object], such as "the mountain possesses that which is qualified by fire-ness" (*vahnitvaviśiṣṭavān parvataḥ*), there fire-ness appears in the form of "possessing fire-ness" by virtue of being explicitly mentioned. The delimitation of the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedakatā*) residing in fire-ness is delimited by "possessing fire-ness."

Where there is a mention of a universal (*jāti*) or an impartite adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), there it appears precisely by way of a property residing in that universal or impartite adjunct. And the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that properties other than universals and impartite adjuncts always appear in some form or other, but never in their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

Experts in categories (*padārthajña*) maintain that the qualifiers (*prakāratā*), the qualificands (*viśeṣyatā*), the objective content (*viṣayatā*), the relation-content (*saṃsargatā*), and the delimiters (*avacchedakatā*) are delimited by various respective properties according to the difference in cognitions, and yet remain undelimited by those same respective properties.
Thus ends the section on technical terminology.
